figures.caption: Disk with a hole

examples.prompt: Three small objects lie in a plane, as shown: 2.0 kg at the origin, 3.0 kg at (4.0 m, 0) and 5.0 kg at (1.0 m, 3.0 m). Find the center of mass of the three-object system.
steps: y_cm = [(2.0)(0) + (3.0)(0) + (5.0)(3.0)]/10.0 = 15/10.0 = 1.5 m. The point lies inside the triangle formed by the objects, closest to the 5.0 kg mass, as it should.

examples.prompt: A 2.0 m rod lies along the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.0 m. Its linear density is λ(x) = 3.0 + 1.5x, with λ in kg/m and x in meters. Find the rod's mass and the position of its center of mass.
examples.answer: M = 9.0 kg; x_cm = 1.1 m (1.11 m), to the right of the midpoint.
steps: x_cm = 10 kg·m/9.0 kg = 1.11 m. The density grows to the right, so the center of mass sits right of the 1.0 m midpoint, as expected.

examples.prompt: A uniform flat disk of radius 0.30 m has a circular hole of radius 0.10 m cut out of it. The hole's center is 0.15 m from the disk's center, as shown. Where is the center of mass of the remaining piece?
examples.answer: On the line through both centers, 0.019 m (1.9 cm) from the disk's center, on the side opposite the hole.
steps: Put the origin at the disk's center with +x toward the hole. Mass is proportional to area, so if the full disk has mass M, the hole has (0.10/0.30)^2 M = M/9.
Treat the hole as negative mass: x_cm = [M(0) − (M/9)(0.15 m)]/(M − M/9).
x_cm = −(0.0167 m)/(8/9) = −0.019 m. The negative sign puts it on the side away from the hole; by symmetry y_cm = 0.

worksheets.title: Particles and composite objects
worksheets.directions: Measure every position from the stated origin. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 1.5 kg ball sits at x = 0 and a 0.50 kg ball sits at x = 2.0 m. Where is the center of mass of the two balls?
steps: The answer is closer to the heavier ball. 1.0 m is the midpoint, which ignores the masses, and 1.5 m swaps the masses.
items.skill: Locate a center of mass in one dimension

items.prompt: The Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10^24 kg and the Moon's is 7.35 × 10^22 kg. Their centers are 3.84 × 10^8 m apart. How far from the Earth's center is the center of mass of the Earth–Moon system? Earth's radius is 6.37 × 10^6 m; is that point inside or outside the Earth?
items.answer: 4.67 × 10^6 m from the Earth's center, which is inside the Earth (about 1.7 × 10^6 m below the surface).
steps: Put the origin at the Earth's center: x_cm = (7.35 × 10^22 kg)(3.84 × 10^8 m)/(5.97 × 10^24 kg + 7.35 × 10^22 kg).
x_cm = 2.82 × 10^31/6.04 × 10^24 = 4.67 × 10^6 m, which is less than 6.37 × 10^6 m, so the point is inside the Earth.
items.skill: Apply the center-of-mass formula to astronomical data

items.prompt: Four small masses sit at the corners of a rectangle: 1.0 kg at (0, 0), 2.0 kg at (3.0 m, 0), 3.0 kg at (3.0 m, 2.0 m) and 4.0 kg at (0, 2.0 m). Find the center of mass.
items.skill: Locate a center of mass in two dimensions

items.prompt: The uniform L-shaped plate shown is made of a bottom strip 0.60 m by 0.20 m and a left strip 0.20 m by 0.40 m. Find the coordinates of its center of mass, and state whether that point lies on the plate.

rubric.criterion: Splits the plate into two rectangles and places each rectangle's mass (proportional to its area, 0.12 m^2 and 0.080 m^2) at its own center, (0.30 m, 0.10 m) and (0.10 m, 0.40 m).
Computes x_cm = y_cm = 0.22 m (accept 0.21–0.23 m).
Concludes that (0.22 m, 0.22 m) lies in the empty corner, off the plate, because both coordinates exceed 0.20 m.

items.answer: (0.22 m, 0.22 m), which is not on the plate: it lies in the empty corner region.
steps: Bottom strip: area 0.12 m^2, center (0.30, 0.10) m; left strip: area 0.080 m^2, center (0.10, 0.40) m. For a uniform plate, mass is proportional to area.
The plate occupies x < 0.20 m or y < 0.20 m, and the point has both coordinates above 0.20 m, so it is in the gap.
items.skill: Find the center of mass of a composite object

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg mass is at (1.0 m, 2.0 m) and a 3.0 kg mass is at (−2.0 m, 1.0 m). Where must a 1.0 kg mass be placed so that the center of mass of all three is at the origin?
steps: The center of mass is at the origin when Σ m_i x_i = 0 and Σ m_i y_i = 0.
items.skill: Work backward from a required center of mass

items.prompt: Which statement about the center of mass is correct?
choices: It is always located where the object has material.
It is the point where the object's mass is evenly split, half on each side, along every line.
It can lie at a point where there is no material, as for a uniform ring.
For two particles, it is always at the midpoint between them.
items.answer: (C) It can lie at a point where there is no material, as for a uniform ring.
steps: A uniform ring's center of mass is at its center by symmetry, and there is no material there.
The center of mass balances moments (mass times distance), not amounts of mass on each side, and it sits at the midpoint of two particles only when their masses are equal.
items.skill: Interpret the meaning of the center of mass

worksheets.title: Continuous objects by integration
worksheets.directions: Rods lie along the x-axis with one end at x = 0. λ is in kg/m and x in meters. Show the integrals you set up. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 1.2 m rod has linear density λ(x) = 2.0x. Find its mass and the position of its center of mass.
steps: M = ∫ from 0 to 1.2 of 2.0x dx = [x^2] from 0 to 1.2 = 1.44 kg.
∫ from 0 to 1.2 of x(2.0x) dx = [(2/3)x^3] from 0 to 1.2 = 1.152 kg·m, so x_cm = 1.152/1.44 = 0.80 m, two-thirds of the way along the rod.
items.skill: Integrate a linear density

items.prompt: A rod's linear density is modeled as λ(x) = A + Bx^2, with λ in kg/m and x in meters. What are the SI units of A and of B? What is the physical meaning of A?
items.answer: A is in kg/m and B is in kg/m^3. A is the linear density at the end x = 0.
steps: Each term must have the units of λ, kg/m. A stands alone, so A is in kg/m; Bx^2 has units B·m^2, so B is in kg/m^3.
At x = 0 the second term vanishes, so λ(0) = A.
items.skill: Check units in a density model

items.prompt: A 3.0 m rod has linear density λ(x) = 4.0 − x, so it is densest at x = 0. Where is its center of mass?
steps: x_cm = 9.0/7.5 = 1.2 m, left of the 1.5 m midpoint because the left end is denser. 9.0 m forgets to divide by M, and 1.8 m mirrors the answer to the wrong side.
items.skill: Find the center of mass of a nonuniform rod

items.prompt: A 2.0 m rod has linear density λ(x) = 0.50 + 0.30x^2. Find its mass and its center of mass.
items.skill: Integrate a quadratic density

items.prompt:
A sensor measures the linear density of a 1.00 m tapered rod at five points:
| x (m) | 0 | 0.25 | 0.50 | 0.75 | 1.00 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| λ (kg/m) | 1.20 | 1.45 | 1.80 | 2.25 | 2.80 |
Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the rod's mass and the position of its center of mass.
steps: x_cm ≈ 1.0875/1.875 = 0.58 m, right of the middle where the rod is denser.
items.skill: Estimate center-of-mass integrals from a table

items.prompt: A 2.0 m rod's linear density increases steadily from 1.0 kg/m at x = 0 to 3.0 kg/m at x = 2.0 m. (a) Write λ(x). (b) Find the rod's mass. (c) Find x_cm. (d) Explain, without calculation, why x_cm is greater than 1.0 m.

rubric.criterion: Writes λ(x) = 1.0 + 1.0x (kg/m) from the two given values.
Finds M = 4.0 kg by integrating λ from 0 to 2.0 m.
Sets up x_cm = (1/M) ∫ x λ dx and gets 1.17 m (accept 1.16–1.18 m).
Explains that more mass lies in the right half, so the mass-weighted average position is right of the midpoint.

items.answer: (a) λ(x) = 1.0 + 1.0x. (b) M = 4.0 kg. (c) x_cm = 1.17 m. (d) The right half is denser, so it carries more of the mass and pulls the average position past the midpoint.
items.skill: Model a density and find its center of mass

worksheets.title: Systems and the center of mass in context
worksheets.directions: Describe the system you choose before you calculate. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A worker pushes a crate across a warehouse floor. Take the system to be the worker and the crate together. List the forces on this system and classify each as internal or external.
items.answer: External: the gravitational forces of the Earth on the worker and on the crate; the floor's normal forces on the worker and on the crate; the floor's friction forces on the worker's shoes and on the crate. Internal: the worker's push on the crate and the crate's push back on the worker.
steps: An external force comes from an object outside the boundary (the Earth or the floor); an internal force is exerted by one part of the system on another.
The worker–crate pushes form an equal and opposite pair inside the system, so they cancel in the sum of forces on the system.
items.skill: Classify internal and external forces

items.prompt: Two carts move on a straight, level track. Cart A (1.0 kg) passes x = 0 at t = 0 moving at a constant +2.0 m/s; cart B (3.0 kg) sits at rest at x = 4.0 m. Write x_cm(t) for the two-cart system before they meet, and find the velocity of the center of mass.
steps: v_cm = dx_cm/dt = 0.50 m/s in the +x direction, which also equals (m_A v_A + m_B v_B)/M = 2.0/4.0.
items.skill: Differentiate a center-of-mass position

items.prompt: A 60 kg paddler stands at the back of a 90 kg canoe floating at rest on still water. He walks 3.0 m forward relative to the canoe. Ignoring water resistance, how far and in which direction does the canoe move relative to the water?
items.answer: 1.2 m backward (opposite the direction the paddler walks).
steps: With no external horizontal force on the paddler–canoe system, its center of mass stays at rest: (60 kg)d_p + (90 kg)d_c = 0, with forward positive.
The paddler moves 3.0 m relative to the canoe: d_p − d_c = 3.0 m. Substituting d_p = 3.0 + d_c gives 180 + 150d_c = 0, so d_c = −1.2 m.
items.skill: Use a stationary center of mass

items.prompt: A rod of length L has linear density λ(x) = kx^2, where k is a constant. Show that its center of mass is at x = 3L/4.
items.answer: M = kL^3/3 and ∫ x λ dx = kL^4/4, so x_cm = (kL^4/4)/(kL^3/3) = 3L/4.
steps: M = ∫ from 0 to L of kx^2 dx = kL^3/3.
∫ from 0 to L of x(kx^2) dx = kL^4/4; dividing gives 3L/4, independent of k.
items.skill: Derive a center of mass symbolically

items.prompt: A hammer is tossed so that it spins as it flies through the air. Neglect air resistance. Which statement describes its motion?
choices: Every point of the hammer follows a parabola.
The heavy head follows a parabola, and the center of mass moves in a straight line.
Only the end of the handle follows a parabola.
The center of mass follows a parabola while the hammer spins around it.
items.answer: (D) The center of mass follows a parabola while the hammer spins around it.
steps: The only external force is gravity, so the center of mass moves like a single projectile: a parabola.
The other points also spin around the center of mass, so their paths are not parabolas.
items.skill: Describe a system's motion by its center of mass

items.prompt: A 1.00 m stick lies along the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 1.00 m. Its linear density is λ(x) = 0.30 + 0.20x, with λ in kg/m and x in meters. A 0.10 kg clip is fastened at x = 0.20 m. At what position should a single support be placed so that the stick and clip balance?

rubric.criterion: Finds the stick's mass, 0.40 kg, by integrating λ.
Finds the stick's moment ∫ x λ dx = 0.217 kg·m.
Adds the clip as a particle: total moment 0.237 kg·m and total mass 0.50 kg.
Identifies the balance point as the center of mass of the whole system.
Gets x = 0.47 m (accept 0.46–0.48 m).

items.answer: At x = 0.47 m, the center of mass of the stick and clip.
steps: x_cm = (0.217 + 0.020)/(0.40 + 0.10) = 0.237/0.50 = 0.47 m; a support there balances the system.
items.skill: Combine a continuous object with a particle

weeks.title: Free-body diagrams and Newton's third and first laws
weeks.objective: Draw free-body diagrams that show each force as an interaction, identify Newton's third-law pairs, and use the first law to solve equilibrium problems by components, including strings at angles and inclines.

connection.before: Week 6's choice of system and Week 2's vector components.
connection.after: Week 8 applies Newton's second law when the net force is not zero, including forces that change with time or position.

days: Forces as interactions: name the object exerting each force; draw free-body diagrams with labeled arrows from one point.
Newton's third law: pair forces on different objects and tell third-law pairs from forces that merely balance.
Newton's first law and inertial frames: zero net force means constant velocity, including rest.
Equilibrium by components: strings at angles, pushes and pulls at angles, and tilted axes on inclines.
Mixed practice with systems of more than one object, then a short check.
explanation: A force is a push or pull that one object exerts on another, so every force has a source. To draw a free-body diagram, isolate the system, then draw one arrow for each force that something outside the system exerts on it. Start each arrow at a single dot (or the center of a box), point it in the force's direction, and label it with its type and source, such as F_N (table on book) or T (rope on crate). Contact forces need contact: a normal force perpendicular to a surface, friction along it, tension along a string. Gravity acts at a distance. Velocity and acceleration are not forces, so they never appear on the diagram, and neither does ma.

Newton's third law says that if object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type. The two forces of a pair act on different objects, so they never appear on the same free-body diagram and never cancel each other. A book resting on a table feels the Earth's gravity and the table's normal force. These balance, but they are not a third-law pair. The partner of the Earth's pull on the book is the book's pull on the Earth, and the partner of the table's push on the book is the book's push on the table.

Newton's first law says that an object's velocity stays constant, in size and direction, exactly when the net force on it is zero. Rest is just the special case v = 0. The law holds in inertial reference frames, which are frames that are not accelerating. In equilibrium, ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0, so the force components must balance in every direction. Choose axes that make the algebra short. On an incline, tilt the axes along and perpendicular to the surface, so that only gravity needs to be split: mg sin θ along the slope and mg cos θ into it.

Common errors: drawing a force that the object exerts on something else; adding a 'force of motion' in the direction of travel; assuming the normal force always equals mg, which fails on inclines and whenever another force has a vertical component; and calling two balanced forces on one object a third-law pair. Another is thinking a moving object needs a net force to keep moving. If a crate slides at constant velocity, the forces on it balance, even though something is pushing it.

Right: the block's free-body diagram as a dot with three labeled arrows: F_g straight down, F_N perpendicular to the incline surface and away from it, and f_s up along the slope. Dashed axes are tilted to lie along and perpendicular to the incline.

figures.alt: A block labeled 4.0 kg on a frictionless incline at 30° to the horizontal. A string runs from the block up along the slope, over a pulley at the top corner, and down to a hanging block of unknown mass m.
figures.caption: Incline and hanging block

figures.caption: Forces on the magnet

figures.alt: Free-body diagram of the book as a dot with three arrows: F_N up, longer than F_g and F_H, which both point down.
figures.caption: Forces on the book

figures.alt: A crate on a level floor pulled to the right by a rope that makes a 30° angle above the horizontal.
figures.caption: Crate pulled by a rope

figures.alt: Free-body diagram of the crate as a dot with four arrows: F_g down, F_N up but shorter than F_g, f_k to the left, and T up and to the right at 30° above the horizontal.
figures.caption: Forces on the crate

examples.prompt: A 40 kg crate is pulled across a level floor at constant velocity by a rope that makes a 30° angle above the horizontal, as shown. The tension in the rope is 120 N. Take +x in the direction of motion and +y up. Draw the free-body diagram, and find the friction force and the normal force on the crate.
examples.answer: Friction 104 N, opposite the motion; normal force 332 N, up.
steps: Forces on the crate: gravity mg = 392 N down, the floor's normal force F_N up, kinetic friction f_k backward, and the tension T at 30° above the horizontal.
Constant velocity means ΣF = 0. In x: T cos 30° − f_k = 0, so f_k = (120 N)(0.866) = 104 N.
In y: F_N + T sin 30° − mg = 0, so F_N = 392 N − 60 N = 332 N. The rope's upward component makes the normal force less than mg.

examples.prompt: Box A (5.0 kg) rests on box B (8.0 kg), which rests on the floor, as shown. List every force on box B with its size and direction, and name the third-law partner of each.
examples.answer: Gravity of the Earth on B: 78 N down (partner: B's pull on the Earth, 78 N up). Normal force of A on B: 49 N down (partner: B's push on A, 49 N up). Normal force of the floor on B: 127 N up (partner: B's push on the floor, 127 N down).
steps: Box A is at rest, so B pushes up on A with m_A g = (5.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 49 N; by the third law, A pushes down on B with 49 N.
Gravity on B is m_B g = (8.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 78.4 N down. B is at rest, so the floor pushes up with 78.4 N + 49 N = 127 N.
Each partner acts on the other object of the interaction (the Earth, A or the floor), has the same size and points the opposite way.

examples.prompt: A 10 kg box is held at rest on a frictionless incline at 30° by a horizontal push F. Take +x horizontal toward the incline and +y up. Find F and the normal force on the box.
examples.answer: F = 57 N; normal force 113 N.
steps: Forces: gravity 98 N down, the push F horizontal, and the normal force F_N perpendicular to the slope, tilted 30° from the vertical (away from the hill).
Vertical: F_N cos 30° = mg, so F_N = 98 N/0.866 = 113 N.
Horizontal: F = F_N sin 30° = (113 N)(0.500) = 57 N, which equals mg tan 30°. Here horizontal and vertical axes are easier than tilted ones, because two of the three forces are already along them.

worksheets.title: Drawing free-body diagrams
worksheets.directions: Draw a free-body diagram before calculating. State your positive directions and use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A book rests on a table. What is the Newton's third-law partner of the Earth's gravitational force on the book?
choices: The table's normal force on the book
The book's gravitational force on the Earth
The book's push on the table
The Earth's push on the table
items.answer: (B) The book's gravitational force on the Earth
steps: A third-law partner involves the same two objects with their roles reversed: the Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls the Earth.
The table's normal force balances gravity here, but it comes from a different interaction (book and table).
items.skill: Identify a third-law pair

items.prompt: A student presses a 3.0 kg textbook against a vertical wall with a horizontal push of 40 N, and the book does not slide. Find the size and direction of the friction force and the normal force on the book. If the push increases to 60 N, what happens to the friction force?
items.answer: Friction 29 N (29.4 N) up; normal force 40 N away from the wall. With a 60 N push, friction stays 29 N; only the normal force grows, to 60 N.
steps: Vertical: the book is at rest, so static friction balances gravity: f_s = mg = (3.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 29.4 N up.
Horizontal: the wall's normal force balances the push, 40 N. A bigger push raises the normal force (and the maximum possible friction), but the friction needed is still mg.
items.skill: Apply equilibrium in two directions

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg lamp hangs from a cord in an elevator that is moving upward at a constant 3.0 m/s. Find the tension in the cord, and explain why the elevator's speed does not matter.
items.answer: 19.6 N. The lamp's velocity is constant, so the net force is zero and T = mg, whatever that constant velocity is.
steps: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by the first law ΣF = 0: T − mg = 0.
T = (2.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 19.6 N; the value of the constant speed never enters.
items.skill: Apply the first law in a moving frame

items.prompt: A hockey puck slides at constant velocity across frictionless ice. Which forces belong on its free-body diagram?
choices: Gravity, the normal force and a forward force that keeps it moving
Gravity and the normal force only
Gravity, the normal force and a backward force from the air
items.answer: (B) Gravity and the normal force only
steps: Only the Earth (gravity) and the ice (normal force) interact with the puck; there is no friction or air resistance here.
No forward force is needed: with zero net force, the first law says the puck keeps its velocity.
items.skill: Choose the forces for a free-body diagram

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball hangs from a string. A steady horizontal wind pushes on the ball with a force of 2.0 N, and the ball hangs at rest with the string at an angle θ from the vertical. Find θ and the tension in the string.
steps: Forces: gravity 4.9 N down, wind 2.0 N horizontal, and tension along the string. Equilibrium gives T sin θ = 2.0 N and T cos θ = 4.9 N.
items.skill: Solve a two-force balance at an angle

items.prompt: A 0.020 kg magnet sticks to a vertical steel refrigerator door. The magnetic attraction between them is 1.5 N. (a) Draw and label a free-body diagram of the magnet. (b) Find the size of each force. (c) For each force, name its third-law partner.

rubric.criterion: Draws four forces on the magnet: gravity down, static friction up, magnetic attraction toward the door and the normal force away from the door.
Finds friction = mg = 0.20 N (0.196 N) and normal force = 1.5 N, from equilibrium in each direction.
Names each partner as a force exerted by the magnet: on the Earth (gravity), and on the door (friction, magnetic attraction and normal force).

items.answer: Gravity 0.20 N down and static friction 0.20 N up; magnetic attraction 1.5 N toward the door and normal force 1.5 N away from it. Partners: the magnet's pull on the Earth; the magnet's friction on the door (down); the magnet's attraction of the door; the magnet's push on the door.
steps: Vertical equilibrium: f_s = mg = (0.020 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 0.196 N. Horizontal equilibrium: F_N = F_M = 1.5 N.
Each partner has the same size, points the opposite way and acts on the other object of the interaction.
items.skill: Draw a diagram and pair every force

worksheets.title: Equilibrium by components
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Choose axes, state them, and write ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 20 kg box sits at rest on a rough ramp inclined at 30°. Using axes along and perpendicular to the ramp, find the static friction force and the normal force on the box.
items.answer: Static friction 98 N up the ramp; normal force 170 N (169.7 N).
steps: Along the ramp: f_s − mg sin 30° = 0, so f_s = (196 N)(0.500) = 98 N.
Perpendicular: F_N − mg cos 30° = 0, so F_N = (196 N)(0.866) = 170 N.
items.skill: Resolve gravity on an incline

items.prompt: A 15 kg crate is pushed across a level floor at constant speed by a force of 90 N directed 20° below the horizontal. Find the kinetic friction force and the normal force on the crate.
items.answer: Friction 85 N (84.6 N), opposite the motion; normal force 178 N.
steps: Horizontal: f_k = (90 N) cos 20° = 84.6 N.
Vertical: F_N = mg + (90 N) sin 20° = 147 N + 30.8 N = 178 N. Pushing downward at an angle increases the normal force.
items.skill: Balance an angled push

items.prompt: The 6.0 kg block shown hangs at rest from two strings. Find the tension in each string.
items.answer: Left string (30°): 43 N; right string (45°): 53 N.
steps: Horizontal: T_L cos 30° = T_R cos 45°. Vertical: T_L sin 30° + T_R sin 45° = (6.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 58.8 N.
From the first equation, T_L = 0.816T_R. Then T_R(0.408 + 0.707) = 58.8 N, so T_R = 52.7 N and T_L = 43.0 N.
The steeper string carries more of the weight.
items.skill: Solve two-string equilibrium

items.prompt: A person stands on a scale in an elevator that is moving downward at constant speed. Compared with the reading when the elevator is at rest, the scale reads
items.answer: (B) the same
steps: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force on the person is zero and the scale's push equals mg.
Only an acceleration changes the reading; the direction of the constant velocity does not matter.
items.skill: Apply the first law to apparent weight

items.prompt: Three horizontal forces act on a ring that stays at rest. F_1 is 30 N in the +x direction and F_2 is 40 N in the +y direction. Find the magnitude and direction of F_3.
items.answer: 50 N at 233° counterclockwise from +x (53° below the −x axis).
steps: Equilibrium: F_3 = −(F_1 + F_2) = (−30 N) i + (−40 N) j.
|F_3| = √(30^2 + 40^2) = 50 N; it points into the third quadrant at 180° + tan^−1(40/30) = 233°.
items.skill: Find a balancing force

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg picture hangs from a wire looped over a single nail. Each side of the wire makes 15° with the horizontal. (a) Find the tension in the wire. (b) Explain why the tension is larger than the picture's weight, and why no amount of tension could make the wire perfectly horizontal.

rubric.criterion: Writes vertical equilibrium for the picture: 2T sin 15° = mg.
Finds T = 38 N (accept 37–39 N).
Explains that only the small vertical component of each side supports the weight, so T must be large.
Explains that a horizontal wire has no vertical component, so 2T sin θ = mg cannot hold for θ = 0 with any finite tension.

items.answer: (a) T = 38 N. (b) Each side supports the picture only through its vertical component, T sin 15°, which is about a quarter of T. As θ → 0, T = mg/(2 sin θ) grows without limit, so a perfectly horizontal wire cannot hold any weight.
steps: Horizontal components cancel by symmetry; vertically 2T sin 15° = (2.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 19.6 N.
T = 19.6 N/(2 × 0.259) = 37.9 N ≈ 38 N, almost twice the weight.
items.skill: Reason about tension at shallow angles

worksheets.title: Third-law pairs and systems
worksheets.directions: Name the system for each diagram. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and state your positive directions. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 2000 kg truck pushes a stalled 1000 kg car along a level road at constant speed. How does the force of the truck on the car compare with the force of the car on the truck?
choices: The truck's force is twice as large.
The truck's force is larger, but not twice as large.
The forces are equal in size.
items.answer: (D) The forces are equal in size.
steps: The two forces are a third-law pair, so they have equal sizes whatever the masses or the motion.
Masses decide how each vehicle responds to the forces on it, not the size of an interaction force.
items.skill: Apply Newton's third law

items.prompt: In a tug-of-war, team A pulls on a light rope with 800 N and the rope does not move. (a) How hard does team B pull on the rope? (b) Later the rope moves toward team A at a constant velocity while team A still pulls with 800 N. How hard does team B pull now? (c) What decides which team moves toward the other?
items.answer: (a) 800 N. (b) Still 800 N. (c) The horizontal forces the ground exerts on each team's feet: a team moves only when the ground's friction on it cannot balance the rope's pull on it.
steps: A light rope at constant velocity (including at rest) has zero net force, so the two pulls on it are equal in size, 800 N, in both cases.
The rope pulls each team with 800 N. Each team's motion depends on the ground's push on its feet, so the team that gets less grip from the ground is dragged.
items.skill: Separate internal and external forces

items.prompt: Block A (3.0 kg) and block B (5.0 kg) are connected by a light string on a level floor. A horizontal force F pulls block B, and block A trails behind. Both slide at a constant velocity. The kinetic friction force is 8.0 N on A and 14 N on B. Find F and the tension in the string.
items.answer: F = 22 N; tension 8.0 N.
steps: System A + B (the tension is internal): F − 8.0 N − 14 N = 0, so F = 22 N.
Block A alone: T − 8.0 N = 0, so T = 8.0 N. Check with B alone: F − T − 14 N = 22 − 8.0 − 14 = 0.
items.skill: Choose systems to find an internal force

items.prompt: A student argues: "When a horse pulls a cart, the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force, so the forces cancel and they can never start moving." Explain the mistake.
items.answer: The two forces act on different objects, so they cannot cancel. Whether the horse speeds up depends only on the forces on the horse: the ground pushes it forward (through friction on its hooves) harder than the cart pulls back. Whether the cart speeds up depends on the forces on the cart: the horse's pull is larger than the friction on the cart.
steps: Third-law pair forces act on different bodies; only forces on the same body add to a net force.
Analyze each body with its own free-body diagram; the ground's horizontal force on the horse is the external force that drives the horse–cart system.
items.skill: Explain why third-law pairs do not cancel

items.prompt: In the figure, a 4.0 kg block rests on a frictionless incline at 30°. A light string parallel to the incline passes over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging block of mass m. The system is at rest. Find the tension in the string and the hanging mass m.
steps: Block on the incline, along the slope: T − (4.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) sin 30° = 0, so T = 19.6 N.
Hanging block: T − mg = 0, so m = 19.6 N/9.8 m/s^2 = 2.0 kg.
items.skill: Solve connected bodies in equilibrium

items.prompt: A 1.2 kg book lies on a level table while a student's hand presses straight down on it with a force of 8.0 N. (a) Draw and label a free-body diagram of the book. (b) Find the normal force from the table. (c) Name the third-law partner of each force on the book. (d) A classmate says the normal force and the gravitational force on the book are a third-law pair. Use this situation to explain why the claim is wrong.

rubric.criterion: Draws three forces: gravity down, the hand's push down and the table's normal force up, with the normal force the longest.
Finds F_N = mg + 8.0 N = 20 N (19.8 N).
Names the partners: the book's pull on the Earth, the book's push up on the hand and the book's push down on the table.
Explains that the two forces act on the same object, come from different interactions (book–Earth and book–table), and here are not even equal (20 N against 12 N), so they cannot be a third-law pair.

items.answer: (b) F_N = 11.8 N + 8.0 N = 20 N (19.8 N). (c) Partners: the book's gravitational pull on the Earth (up), the book's push on the hand (up) and the book's push on the table (down). (d) Third-law partners act on different objects and are always equal; here both forces act on the book, come from different interactions, and differ (20 N against 12 N).
steps: Equilibrium of the book: F_N − mg − F_hand = 0, with mg = (1.2 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 11.8 N.
F_N = 11.8 N + 8.0 N = 19.8 N ≈ 20 N, which differs from mg, so the two forces cannot be a third-law pair.
items.skill: Distinguish balanced forces from third-law pairs

weeks.title: Newton's second law with variable forces
weeks.objective: Apply ΣF = ma to single objects and connected systems, integrate a time-dependent force to find velocity and position, and use a = v dv/dx to find speed as a function of position for a position-dependent force.

connection.before: Week 7's free-body diagrams and Week 1's antiderivatives and definite integrals.
connection.after: Week 9 supplies the force laws for gravity, friction and springs to use with the second law.

days: The second law as a = ΣF/m for a chosen system; component equations; apparent weight in elevators.
Connected objects: shared accelerations, tension and contact forces, and choosing the whole system or one part.
Time-dependent forces: a(t) = F(t)/m, then integrate for v(t) and x(t); area under a force–time graph.
Position-dependent forces: the chain rule a = v dv/dx and ½v^2 − ½v_0^2 = (1/m) ∫ F dx.
Mixed practice deciding which form of the second law a problem needs, then a short check.
explanation: Newton's second law says that the net external force on a system equals the system's mass times its acceleration: ΣF = ma, or a = ΣF/m. It is a vector law, so it holds component by component: ΣF_x = ma_x and ΣF_y = ma_y. The method is the same every time. Choose the system, draw its free-body diagram, choose axes (one along the acceleration if you know its direction), write one equation per axis, and solve. For objects joined by a taut string or pushing on each other, the parts share one acceleration. The whole system then gives the acceleration quickly, because the internal tension or contact force cancels. A single part gives that internal force. Tension in an accelerating string is not equal to a hanging object's weight; it is less when the object accelerates downward and more when it accelerates upward.

When the force changes with time, the acceleration does too, and the constant-acceleration equations no longer apply. Integrate instead. From a(t) = F(t)/m, the velocity is v(t) = v_0 + (1/m) ∫ from 0 to t of F dt, and integrating v(t) gives the position. On a graph of F against t, the area under the curve, in N·s, divided by the mass gives the change in velocity. Velocity keeps increasing as long as the force is positive, even while the force is shrinking, so the greatest speed comes where the force changes sign.

When the force depends on position, as with a spring or a variable push, you know a as a function of x, but a = dv/dt is a rate with respect to time. The chain rule connects the two: a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx. (Calculus courses meet the chain rule a little later; here is the only form we need.) Because v dv/dx is the derivative of ½v^2 with respect to x, Newton's law becomes d(½v^2)/dx = F(x)/m. Integrating from x_0 to x gives ½v^2 − ½v_0^2 = (1/m) ∫ from x_0 to x of F dx. So the area under a force–position graph tells you how ½v^2 changes. Unit 3 will call this area work.

Common errors: using mg as the tension in a string that accelerates; leaving out a force's sign; applying v^2 = v_0^2 + 2aΔx with one value of a when a varies; integrating a force of x with respect to t (or a force of t with respect to x); and forgetting the starting velocity when you evaluate an integral. Check units: (N·s)/kg = m/s and (N·m)/kg = m^2/s^2.

figures.caption: Area under a force–time graph

examples.prompt: In the figure, block A (3.0 kg) sits on a frictionless table and is tied by a light string, over a light frictionless pulley, to block B (2.0 kg), which hangs freely. The blocks are released from rest. Find their acceleration and the tension in the string.
examples.answer: a = 3.9 m/s^2 (A toward the pulley, B downward); T = 12 N.
steps: Take the direction of motion as positive for each block: right for A, down for B. Both have the same size of acceleration a.
System A + B: the only unbalanced external force along the motion is B's weight, (2.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 19.6 N, so a = 19.6 N/5.0 kg = 3.92 m/s^2.
Block A alone: T = m_A a = (3.0 kg)(3.92 m/s^2) = 11.8 N ≈ 12 N, less than B's 19.6 N weight because B accelerates downward.

examples.prompt: A 4.0 kg cart starts from rest at x = 0 on a frictionless track. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.0 s, the net force on it is F(t) = 6.0t − 1.5t^2, with F in newtons, t in seconds and +x positive. Find v(t), and the cart's velocity and position at t = 4.0 s.
steps: v(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of a dt = 0.75t^2 − 0.125t^3, so v(4.0) = 12 − 8.0 = 4.0 m/s. This equals the shaded area, 16 N·s, divided by 4.0 kg.

examples.prompt: A 0.50 kg puck slides along +x on frictionless ice. At x = 0 its speed is 2.0 m/s. A variable push then gives a net force F(x) = 3.0x − 0.80x^2, with F in newtons and x in meters. Find the puck's speed at x = 3.0 m.
steps: Use a = v dv/dx: d(½v^2)/dx = F(x)/m, so ½v^2 − ½v_0^2 = (1/m) ∫ from 0 to 3.0 of F dx.

worksheets.title: The second law with constant forces
worksheets.directions: Draw a free-body diagram for each system you use. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and state your positive directions. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: Two forces act on a 2.0 kg object: 6.0 N east and 8.0 N north. What is the magnitude of the object's acceleration?
steps: The net force is the vector sum: |ΣF| = √(6.0^2 + 8.0^2) = 10 N.
a = 10 N/2.0 kg = 5.0 m/s^2. 7.0 m/s^2 adds the magnitudes, and 10 m/s^2 forgets to divide by the mass.
items.skill: Apply the second law to a vector sum

items.prompt: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator. Take up as positive. Find the scale reading (a) while the elevator speeds up moving upward at 1.5 m/s^2, and (b) while it slows to a stop moving upward at 2.0 m/s^2.
steps: Person: F_N − mg = ma, so F_N = m(g + a).
(a) a = +1.5 m/s^2: F_N = 60(11.3) = 678 N. (b) Slowing while moving up means a points down: a = −2.0 m/s^2, so F_N = 60(7.8) = 468 N.
items.skill: Find apparent weight from the acceleration

items.prompt: In the figure, a horizontal force F = 24 N pushes block A (4.0 kg), which pushes block B (2.0 kg) across a frictionless floor. Find the acceleration and the force A exerts on B. Then find that contact force if the same 24 N pushes on B from the right instead.
items.answer: a = 4.0 m/s^2; A pushes B with 8.0 N. Pushing from the right, the contact force is 16 N.
steps: Both blocks: a = 24 N/6.0 kg = 4.0 m/s^2.
Block B alone: F_AB = m_B a = (2.0 kg)(4.0 m/s^2) = 8.0 N. Pushed from the right, the contact force must accelerate A instead: (4.0 kg)(4.0 m/s^2) = 16 N.
items.skill: Find a contact force between accelerating blocks

items.prompt: A block slides from rest down a frictionless ramp inclined at 20°. Find its acceleration and the time it takes to travel 2.0 m along the ramp.
steps: Along the ramp: ma = mg sin 20°, so a = (9.8 m/s^2)(0.342) = 3.35 m/s^2.
With constant a from rest, 2.0 m = ½(3.35 m/s^2)t^2, so t = √(4.0/3.35) = 1.09 s ≈ 1.1 s.
items.skill: Apply the second law on an incline

items.prompt: A 3.0 kg block and a 5.0 kg block hang on opposite sides of a light, frictionless pulley and are released from rest. What is the tension in the string?
steps: System: a = (5.0 − 3.0)(9.8)/8.0 = 2.45 m/s^2, with the 5.0 kg block moving down.
3.0 kg block: T − (3.0)(9.8) = (3.0)(2.45), so T = 36.8 N ≈ 37 N. It lies between the two weights (29 N and 49 N); 39 N is their plain average.
items.skill: Find tension in an accelerating system

items.prompt: A 10 kg crate is lifted by a vertical rope of mass 1.0 kg. The crate and rope accelerate upward at 0.80 m/s^2. (a) Find the tension at the bottom of the rope, where it is tied to the crate. (b) Find the tension at the top of the rope, where it is pulled. (c) Explain why the two tensions differ.

rubric.criterion: Applies the second law to the crate alone: T_bottom − mg = ma.
Finds T_bottom = 106 N (accept 105–107 N).
Applies the second law to crate plus rope (11 kg) and finds T_top = 117 N (accept 116–118 N).
Explains that the top must also support and accelerate the rope's own mass, which needs (1.0 kg)(g + a) = 11 N more.

items.answer: (a) 106 N. (b) 117 N. (c) The extra 11 N at the top supports the rope's weight and gives the rope its acceleration; only a massless rope has the same tension everywhere.
steps: Crate: T_bottom = (10 kg)(9.8 + 0.80) m/s^2 = 106 N.
Crate + rope: T_top = (11 kg)(10.6 m/s^2) = 116.6 N ≈ 117 N.
items.skill: Analyze tension in a rope with mass

worksheets.title: Forces that depend on time
worksheets.directions: Take +x along the force when it is positive. Show each integral you evaluate. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg object starts from rest at x = 0 on a frictionless surface. The net force on it is F(t) = 2.0t, with F in newtons and t in seconds. Find its velocity and position at t = 2.0 s.
steps: a = F/m = 4.0t, so v = ∫ from 0 to t of 4.0t dt = 2.0t^2 and v(2.0) = 8.0 m/s.
items.skill: Integrate a time-dependent force twice

items.prompt: The graph shows the net force on a 2.0 kg cart, which moves at +1.0 m/s at t = 0. Find the cart's velocity at t = 6.0 s, and the time interval in which its acceleration is greatest.
items.answer: v(6.0 s) = +17 m/s. The acceleration is greatest, 4.0 m/s^2, from t = 2.0 s to 4.0 s, where the force is largest.
steps: Area under F–t: triangle ½(2.0)(8.0) = 8.0 N·s, rectangle (2.0)(8.0) = 16 N·s and triangle 8.0 N·s, a total of 32 N·s.
Δv = 32 N·s/2.0 kg = 16 m/s, so v = 1.0 + 16 = 17 m/s. The largest force, 8.0 N, gives a = 8.0/2.0 = 4.0 m/s^2.
items.skill: Read velocity change from a force–time graph

items.prompt: A force is modeled as F(t) = At − Bt^3, with F in newtons and t in seconds. What are the SI units of A and B?
items.answer: A in N/s and B in N/s^3.
steps: Each term must be in newtons: At has units A·s, so A is in N/s.
Bt^3 has units B·s^3, so B is in N/s^3.
items.skill: Check units in a force model

items.prompt: A 3.0 kg block starts from rest at x = 0 on a frictionless surface. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 6.0 s the net force on it is F(t) = 12 − 3.0t, with F in newtons and t in seconds. (a) When is the block's speed greatest, and what is that speed? (b) Find its velocity at t = 6.0 s. (c) Where is it at the time of greatest speed?
steps: v(t) = (1/3.0) ∫ from 0 to t of (12 − 3.0t) dt = 4.0t − 0.50t^2. The velocity stops increasing when F = 0, at t = 4.0 s: v(4.0) = 16 − 8.0 = 8.0 m/s.
v(6.0) = 24 − 18 = 6.0 m/s; the negative force after 4.0 s slows the block.
items.skill: Find a maximum speed under a changing force

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg object moves along a line with velocity v(t) = 3.0t^2 − t^3, with v in m/s and t in seconds. What is the net force on it at t = 1.0 s?
steps: F = ma = (2.0 kg)(3.0 m/s^2) = 6.0 N. 3.0 N is the acceleration's value, and 4.0 N is m times the velocity.
items.skill: Differentiate velocity to find force

items.prompt: A 1200 kg car starts from rest. Its net forward force is F(t) = 3600 − 400t, with F in newtons and t in seconds, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 9.0 s. (a) Sketch the car's acceleration against time. (b) Find its speed at t = 9.0 s. (c) Find the distance it covers in those 9.0 s. (d) Explain why v^2 = 2aΔx with a single value of a cannot be used here.

rubric.criterion: Sketches a straight line falling from 3.0 m/s^2 at t = 0 to 0 at t = 9.0 s.
Integrates a(t) = 3.0 − t/3 to get v(t) = 3.0t − t^2/6.
Finds v(9.0 s) = 13.5 m/s (accept 13–14 m/s).
Integrates v(t) to get 81 m (accept 80–82 m).
Explains that the acceleration changes with time, so no single a describes the motion.

items.answer: (a) a(t) = 3.0 − t/3, a line from 3.0 m/s^2 down to 0 at 9.0 s. (b) 13.5 m/s. (c) 81 m. (d) The constant-acceleration equations assume one fixed value of a; here a falls steadily, so they give wrong results.
items.skill: Integrate a decreasing force and interpret the result

worksheets.title: Forces that depend on position
worksheets.directions: Use a = v dv/dx, so that ½v^2 − ½v_0^2 = (1/m) ∫ F dx. Take +x as positive. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A cart's position is x(t) = 2.0t^2 + 1.0, with x in meters and t in seconds, for t ≥ 0. Find a = dv/dt. Then write ½v^2 as a function of x, differentiate it with respect to x, and show that you get the same acceleration.
items.answer: a = 4.0 m/s^2. Since v = 4.0t and t^2 = (x − 1.0)/2.0, ½v^2 = 8.0t^2 = 4.0(x − 1.0), whose derivative with respect to x is 4.0 m/s^2.
steps: v = dx/dt = 4.0t and a = dv/dt = 4.0 m/s^2.
½v^2 = 8.0t^2 = 4.0(x − 1.0), and d(½v^2)/dx = 4.0, which equals v dv/dx = a.
items.skill: Verify a = v dv/dx

items.prompt: A 1.0 kg block starts from rest at x = 0 on a frictionless surface. The net force on it is F(x) = 6.0 − 2.0x, with F in newtons and x in meters. (a) Find its speed at x = 3.0 m. (b) Explain why this is its greatest speed. (c) Where does it momentarily stop?
items.answer: (a) 4.2 m/s. (b) The force is positive for x < 3.0 m and negative beyond, so the block speeds up until x = 3.0 m and slows afterward. (c) At x = 6.0 m.
steps: It stops where ∫ from 0 to X of (6.0 − 2.0x) dx = 6.0X − X^2 = 0, at X = 6.0 m.
items.skill: Use a position-dependent force

items.prompt: The graph shows the net force on a 2.0 kg object that moves at +3.0 m/s as it passes x = 0. Find its speed at x = 5.0 m and its greatest speed between x = 0 and x = 5.0 m.
items.answer: 5.6 m/s at x = 5.0 m; the greatest speed is 5.7 m/s, at x = 4.0 m.
steps: Area from 0 to 4.0 m: rectangle (2.0)(8.0) = 16 N·m plus triangle ½(2.0)(8.0) = 8.0 N·m, a total of 24 N·m; from 4.0 to 5.0 m the area is ½(1.0)(−4.0) = −2.0 N·m.
The speed is greatest where F changes sign, at 4.0 m: ½v^2 = 4.5 + 24/2.0 = 16.5, so v = 5.7 m/s.
items.skill: Use the area under a force–position graph

items.prompt: A net force F(x) that changes with position acts on an object of mass m moving along x. Which relation is correct?
steps: With a = v dv/dx = d(½v^2)/dx, integrating F/m over x changes ½v^2.
The first choice mixes in an integral over x where one over t is needed, and the third uses the starting force as if it were constant.
items.skill: Choose the correct integral form of the second law

items.prompt: A 0.20 kg bead slides along a frictionless horizontal wire. It passes x = 0 moving at +6.0 m/s, and from there a retarding force F(x) = −1.8x^2 acts on it, with F in newtons and x in meters. How far does it travel before it stops?
items.skill: Find a stopping distance for a variable force

items.prompt: A 1.6 kg cart moves along +x. Its velocity is measured to depend on position as v(x) = 2.0 + 0.50x, with v in m/s and x in meters, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4.0 m. (a) Find the cart's acceleration as a function of x. (b) Find the net force on the cart at x = 2.0 m. (c) A student says the acceleration must be zero because v increases by the same amount for every meter. Explain the error. (d) Is the acceleration constant? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Uses a = v dv/dx with dv/dx = 0.50 s^−1.
Explains that a constant dv/dx is a change per meter, not per second; since the cart covers each meter faster, v changes faster in time.
States that a grows with x (and with time), so it is not constant.

items.answer: (a) a = v dv/dx = (2.0 + 0.50x)(0.50) = 1.0 + 0.25x. (b) 2.4 N. (c) Acceleration is dv/dt, not dv/dx; as the cart speeds up it crosses each meter in less time, so the same gain per meter is a growing gain per second. (d) No: a rises from 1.0 m/s^2 at x = 0 to 2.0 m/s^2 at x = 4.0 m.
steps: dv/dx = 0.50 per second, so a = v(0.50) = 1.0 + 0.25x.
At x = 2.0 m: a = 1.5 m/s^2 and F = ma = 2.4 N.
items.skill: Connect a velocity–position model to force

weeks.title: Gravitational, friction, and spring forces
weeks.objective: Use Newton's law of gravitation and the gravitational field g = GM/r^2, model static and kinetic friction, and apply Hooke's law to single springs and to springs in series and parallel, combining these forces with Newton's second law.

connection.before: Week 8's second law and Week 7's free-body diagrams.
connection.after: Week 10 adds forces that depend on speed, such as drag, and the terminal speed they produce.

days: Newton's law of gravitation, the field g = GM/r^2, weight at altitude and on other planets, and mass versus weight.
Static friction as a force that adjusts up to μ_s F_N; kinetic friction μ_k F_N; friction against applied-force graphs.
Friction on inclines and in accelerating vehicles; the angle at which a block starts to slip.
Hooke's law F_s = −kΔx; finding k from data; springs in series and in parallel.
Mixed problems that combine gravity, friction and springs with the second law, then a short check.
explanation: Any two masses attract each other. The size of the force is F_g = Gm_1m_2/r^2, where r is the distance between their centers and G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2. For a spherical planet of mass M, the force on a mass m at distance r from the center is m(GM/r^2), so the gravitational field there is g = GM/r^2. Near Earth's surface, with M = 5.97 × 10^24 kg and R = 6.37 × 10^6 m, this gives the familiar 9.8 m/s^2. Field strength falls as 1/r^2: at an altitude equal to one Earth radius, r doubles and g drops to a quarter. Weight mg changes from place to place, but mass does not.

Friction acts along a surface and opposes sliding, or the sliding that would happen without it. Kinetic friction acts while surfaces slide and has the size f_k = μ_k F_N. Static friction acts while they do not slide. It takes whatever value, up to a maximum μ_s F_N, keeps the surfaces together, so f_s ≤ μ_s F_N, and usually μ_s > μ_k. The coefficients have no units. As you push harder on a resting crate, the static friction rises to match the push until it reaches μ_s F_N; then the crate breaks free and the friction drops to μ_k F_N. On an incline with no other forces along it, a block starts to slip when tan θ = μ_s, because mg sin θ = μ_s mg cos θ there.

An ideal spring exerts a force proportional to its stretch or compression Δx from its natural length: F_s = −kΔx. The minus sign means the force points back toward the natural length, and the spring constant k, in N/m, measures stiffness. A graph of force against stretch is a straight line through the origin with slope k. Two springs in parallel share the load and stretch the same amount, so k_eq = k_1 + k_2. Two springs in series carry the same force and their stretches add, so 1/k_eq = 1/k_1 + 1/k_2. A light spring has the same tension along its whole length, even when it accelerates.

Common errors: measuring r from a planet's surface instead of its center; writing f_s = μ_s F_N when the surface is not about to slip; assuming F_N = mg when another force or an incline changes it; reversing the direction of friction (it opposes relative sliding, so it can point forward, as on a crate in a truck that speeds up); and giving a spring force the wrong sign. Check the size of each answer too: gravity between everyday objects is tiny, and a coefficient of friction above about 1.5 is unusual.

figures.alt: Graph of friction force on a 3.0 kg crate against horizontal applied force, both from 0 to 20 N. The friction rises along a straight line where friction equals the applied force up to 14 N at an applied force of 14 N, then drops to 10 N and stays at 10 N for larger applied forces.
figures.caption: Friction on a crate as the push increases

figures.alt: A block on a rough incline that rises to the right at 30°. An arrow labeled v_0 points up along the slope from the block.
figures.caption: Block sent up a rough incline

figures.alt: Left: two springs labeled k_1 and k_2 hang one below the other from a ceiling, with a block at the bottom. Right: two springs labeled k_1 and k_2 hang side by side from a ceiling, both attached to a horizontal bar that holds a block.
figures.caption: Springs in series (left) and in parallel (right)

figures.alt: Free-body diagram of the block on the incline as a dot with three arrows: F_g straight down, F_N perpendicular to the slope, and f_k pointing down along the slope. Dashed axes lie along and perpendicular to the slope.
figures.caption: Forces while the block slides up

examples.prompt: A 1200 kg satellite orbits 600 km above Earth's surface. Find the gravitational field strength at that altitude and the gravitational force on the satellite. Use G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2, M_E = 5.97 × 10^24 kg and R_E = 6.37 × 10^6 m.
examples.answer: g = 8.20 m/s^2; F_g = 9.84 × 10^3 N, toward Earth's center.
steps: Measure r from Earth's center: r = 6.37 × 10^6 m + 0.60 × 10^6 m = 6.97 × 10^6 m.
F_g = mg = (1200 kg)(8.20 m/s^2) = 9.84 × 10^3 N. The satellite is not weightless; it is in free fall around the Earth.

examples.prompt: An 8.0 kg box rests on a level floor with μ_s = 0.45 and μ_k = 0.30. A rope pulls on it with 50 N at 25° above the horizontal. Take +x along the horizontal part of the pull and +y up. Does the box move? If so, find its acceleration.
examples.answer: Yes. The box slides with a = 3.5 m/s^2 in the +x direction.
steps: Vertical: F_N = mg − (50 N) sin 25° = 78.4 N − 21.1 N = 57.3 N.
Horizontal pull: (50 N) cos 25° = 45.3 N, more than the maximum static friction μ_s F_N = 0.45(57.3 N) = 25.8 N, so the box slides.

examples.prompt: A 0.40 kg block hangs at rest from two identical springs, each with k = 120 N/m. Find how far the block hangs below the springs' unstretched position when the springs are (a) in series and (b) in parallel, as shown.
steps: The load is mg = (0.40 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 3.92 N.
(a) In series each spring carries 3.92 N, and the stretches add: k_eq = (1/120 + 1/120)^−1 = 60 N/m, so Δx = 3.92/60 = 0.065 m.
(b) In parallel the springs share the load and stretch equally: k_eq = 240 N/m, so Δx = 3.92/240 = 0.016 m.

worksheets.title: Gravitational force and field
worksheets.directions: Use G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2, M_E = 5.97 × 10^24 kg and R_E = 6.37 × 10^6 m. Measure distances between centers. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: Two asteroids attract each other with a gravitational force F. If both masses are doubled and the distance between their centers is tripled, the force becomes
steps: F ∝ m_1m_2/r^2: doubling both masses multiplies F by 4, and tripling r divides it by 9.
The new force is 4F/9. 2F/9 doubles only one mass, and 4F/3 divides by 3 instead of 3^2.
items.skill: Scale the law of gravitation

items.prompt: Jupiter's moon Ganymede has a mass of 1.48 × 10^23 kg and a radius of 2.63 × 10^6 m. A 75 kg lander touches down on it. Find the gravitational field strength at Ganymede's surface, the lander's weight there, and how many times larger its weight would be on Earth.
items.answer: g = 1.43 m/s^2; weight 107 N; its weight on Earth (735 N) is 6.9 times larger.
steps: Weight = mg = (75 kg)(1.43 m/s^2) = 107 N; on Earth it is (75)(9.8) = 735 N, which is 9.8/1.43 = 6.9 times larger. The lander's mass is 75 kg in both places.
items.skill: Compute surface gravity of a moon

items.prompt: At what altitude above Earth's surface is the gravitational field strength half its surface value?
steps: Altitude h = r − R_E = 0.414 R_E = 2.64 × 10^6 m.
items.skill: Use the inverse-square dependence of g

items.prompt: A 4.0 kg sphere has its center at x = 0 and a 9.0 kg sphere has its center at x = 1.0 m. At what point between them would a small test mass feel zero net gravitational force from the two spheres?
items.answer: At x = 0.40 m.
steps: Zero net force needs G(4.0)m/x^2 = G(9.0)m/(1.0 − x)^2.
Taking square roots: 2.0/x = 3.0/(1.0 − x), so 2.0 − 2.0x = 3.0x and x = 0.40 m, closer to the smaller mass.
items.skill: Locate a point of zero gravitational force

items.prompt: Two 5.0 kg bowling balls sit with their centers 0.30 m apart. Find the gravitational force between them and compare it with the weight of one ball.
items.answer: 1.9 × 10^−8 N, about 3.8 × 10^−10 of one ball's 49 N weight.
steps: Weight = (5.0)(9.8) = 49 N; the ratio is 1.85 × 10^−8/49 = 3.8 × 10^−10, so the balls' mutual attraction is negligible.
items.skill: Judge the size of everyday gravitational forces

items.prompt: The gravitational field at distance r from Earth's center is g(r) = GM/r^2. (a) Find dg/dr. (b) Use it to show that at a small altitude h, g ≈ g_0(1 − 2h/R), where g_0 is the surface value and R is Earth's radius. (c) By what percentage is g smaller at an altitude of 10 km than at the surface?

rubric.criterion: Differentiates with the power rule: dg/dr = −2GM/r^3.
Uses Δg ≈ (dg/dr)h at r = R and rewrites −2GMh/R^3 as −g_0(2h/R).
Finds a decrease of 0.31% (accept 0.30–0.32%) at 10 km.

steps: g = GMr^−2, so dg/dr = −2GMr^−3.
Near r = R a small change h gives Δg ≈ (dg/dr)h, and GM/R^2 = g_0.
items.skill: Use a derivative to approximate a small change

worksheets.title: Static and kinetic friction
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Decide first whether the surfaces slide. State your positive directions and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 5.0 kg block rests on a level floor with μ_s = 0.50 and μ_k = 0.35. Find the friction force and the block's acceleration when a horizontal push of (a) 20 N and (b) 30 N is applied.
items.answer: (a) Friction 20 N, opposite the push; a = 0. (b) Friction 17 N (17.2 N); a = 2.6 m/s^2 in the direction of the push.
steps: Maximum static friction: μ_s mg = 0.50(49 N) = 24.5 N.
(a) 20 N < 24.5 N, so static friction matches the push and the block stays at rest.
items.skill: Decide between static and kinetic friction

items.prompt: The graph shows the friction force on a 3.0 kg crate on a level floor as a horizontal push slowly increases. Find μ_s and μ_k.
steps: F_N = mg = 29.4 N. The friction peaks at 14 N, the largest static friction: μ_s = 14/29.4 = 0.48.
Once the crate slides, the friction is a steady 10 N: μ_k = 10/29.4 = 0.34.
items.skill: Read coefficients of friction from a graph

items.prompt: A block rests on a board whose angle θ is slowly raised. For the block and board, μ_s = 0.60 and μ_k = 0.45. (a) At what angle does the block start to slip? (b) What is its acceleration if the board is held at that angle while it slides?
items.answer: (a) 31°; (b) 1.3 m/s^2 down the slope.
steps: (a) Slipping starts when mg sin θ = μ_s mg cos θ, so tan θ = 0.60 and θ = 31°.
items.skill: Analyze friction on a tilting incline

items.prompt: A crate rides in the bed of a pickup truck without slipping while the truck speeds up in the forward direction. What is the direction of the friction force that the truck bed exerts on the crate?
choices: There is no friction, because the crate does not slide.
items.answer: (B) Forward
steps: The crate speeds up forward with the truck, so the net force on it must point forward.
The only horizontal force on the crate is static friction from the bed, so it points forward; it opposes the sliding that would happen without it.
items.skill: Determine the direction of static friction

items.prompt: In the situation of a crate in a truck bed, μ_s = 0.40 between the crate and the bed. What is the largest forward acceleration the truck can have without the crate slipping?
steps: Static friction is the net force on the crate: ma ≤ μ_s mg.
a_max = μ_s g = 0.40(9.8 m/s^2) = 3.9 m/s^2, independent of the crate's mass.
items.skill: Find a maximum acceleration from μ_s

items.prompt: A 4.0 kg block is launched up a rough incline at 30° with an initial speed of 6.0 m/s, as shown. The coefficients are μ_k = 0.25 and μ_s = 0.40. (a) Draw a free-body diagram of the block while it moves up the slope. (b) Find the size of its acceleration as it moves up. (c) How far up the slope does it travel? (d) Does it slide back down? If so, find its acceleration on the way down.

rubric.criterion: Draws gravity down, the normal force perpendicular to the slope and kinetic friction down the slope.
Finds a = g(sin 30° + μ_k cos 30°) = 7.0 m/s^2 (accept 6.9–7.1 m/s^2), directed down the slope.
Finds a distance of 2.6 m (accept 2.5–2.6 m) from v^2 = v_0^2 − 2ad.
Compares mg sin 30° with μ_s mg cos 30° (or tan 30° = 0.58 > 0.40) to conclude that it slides back.
Finds a = g(sin 30° − μ_k cos 30°) = 2.8 m/s^2 down the slope.

items.answer: (b) 7.0 m/s^2 down the slope. (c) 2.6 m. (d) Yes: tan 30° = 0.58 exceeds μ_s = 0.40, so static friction cannot hold it, and it slides down at 2.8 m/s^2.
steps: Up the slope, both gravity's component and kinetic friction point down the slope: a = 9.8(0.500 + 0.25 × 0.866) = 7.02 m/s^2.
On the way down, friction points up the slope: a = 9.8(0.500 − 0.217) = 2.78 m/s^2.
items.skill: Analyze motion up and down a rough incline

worksheets.title: Springs and combined forces
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Treat springs as light and ideal. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt:
A student hangs weights from a spring and records the stretch:
| F (N) | 0 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Δx (cm) | 0 | 2.4 | 4.9 | 7.5 | 9.9 |
Describe how a graph of F against Δx tests Hooke's law, and find the spring constant.
items.answer: The points lie close to a straight line through the origin, as Hooke's law requires; its slope gives k ≈ 40 N/m.
steps: Hooke's law, F = kΔx, gives a straight line through the origin with slope k when F is plotted against Δx in meters.
A best-fit line through the origin passes near (0.099 m, 4.0 N), so k ≈ 4.0 N/0.099 m = 40 N/m.
items.skill: Find a spring constant from data

items.prompt: Springs with k_1 = 300 N/m and k_2 = 600 N/m support an 18 N load. Find the total stretch when they are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel, with the load placed so that the bar stays level, as in the figure.
items.skill: Combine springs in series and parallel

items.prompt: A spring with spring constant k is cut into two equal halves. What is the spring constant of each half?
items.answer: (D) 2k
steps: Under the same force, each half stretches half as much as the whole spring did.
k = F/Δx, so halving Δx at the same F doubles the constant: 2k. Equivalently, two halves in series must give k.
items.skill: Reason about spring constants

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg block on a level surface is attached to a horizontal spring with k = 200 N/m. The block is pulled 0.15 m from the spring's natural length and released. Find its initial acceleration (a) if the surface is frictionless and (b) if μ_k = 0.20 and the block starts to slide.
items.answer: (a) 60 m/s^2 toward the natural length; (b) 58 m/s^2 toward the natural length.
steps: Spring force: kΔx = (200 N/m)(0.15 m) = 30 N toward the natural length. (a) a = 30/0.50 = 60 m/s^2.
(b) Kinetic friction opposes the motion: f_k = 0.20(0.50)(9.8) = 0.98 N, so a = (30 − 0.98)/0.50 = 58 m/s^2.
items.skill: Combine spring and friction forces

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg block rests on a frictionless incline at 35°, held by a spring parallel to the slope and attached above it, with k = 150 N/m. How much is the spring stretched?
items.answer: 7.5 cm
steps: Along the slope: kΔx = mg sin 35° = (2.0)(9.8)(0.574) = 11.2 N.
items.skill: Balance a spring on an incline

items.prompt: Block A (1.0 kg) and block B (3.0 kg) sit on a frictionless table, joined by a light spring with k = 250 N/m. A constant 12 N force pulls A horizontally away from B, and after a short time both blocks accelerate together with a steady spring stretch. (a) Find the common acceleration. (b) Find the spring force and the stretch. (c) The same 12 N force is instead applied to B, pulling it away from A. Find the new stretch. (d) Explain why the stretch differs.

rubric.criterion: Finds a = 12 N/4.0 kg = 3.0 m/s^2 from the whole system.
Applies the second law to B alone: spring force 9.0 N.
Finds a stretch of 3.6 cm (accept 3.5–3.7 cm).
Finds a spring force of 3.0 N on A and a stretch of 1.2 cm when B is pulled.
Explains that the spring must accelerate whichever block trails, so the stretch is larger when the trailing block is heavier.

items.answer: (a) 3.0 m/s^2. (b) 9.0 N; 3.6 cm. (c) 1.2 cm. (d) The spring supplies the whole net force on the trailing block, so it must pull harder, and stretch more, when that block has more mass.
steps: Pulling B: the spring pulls A with (1.0)(3.0) = 3.0 N, so Δx = 3.0/250 = 0.012 m.
items.skill: Analyze a spring inside an accelerating system

weeks.title: Resistive forces and terminal speed
weeks.objective: Model resistive forces that depend on speed, find terminal speed, describe the exponential approach to it, verify a proposed velocity function by substituting it into Newton's second law, and analyze supplied terminal-speed data.

connection.before: Week 8's second law with variable forces and Week 9's force models.
connection.after: Week 11 applies the second law along a curved path in circular motion and closes Unit 2.

days: Resistive forces: the linear model bv and the quadratic model cv^2; free-body diagrams of a falling object at different speeds.
Terminal speed from ΣF = 0; how acceleration falls as speed rises; reading velocity–time graphs.
The exponential function: d/dt e^(kt) = k e^(kt), checked numerically; verify v(t) = v_T(1 − e^(−t/τ)) by substitution; the time constant τ = m/b.
Coasting against drag, v = v_0 e^(−t/τ), and the distance it covers; quadratic drag and how terminal speed scales with mass.
Paper investigation with supplied terminal-speed data, then a short check.
explanation: A resistive force, such as air resistance or the drag of a liquid, points opposite an object's velocity and grows with its speed. Two models cover most cases. A small, slow object in a thick fluid, such as a bead sinking in oil, feels a drag proportional to speed: F = −bv, with b in kg/s. A larger, faster object in air, such as a skydiver, feels a drag proportional to the square of the speed, of size cv^2 with c in kg/m. Because the force depends on v, Newton's second law becomes an equation that links v to its own rate of change. For an object falling with linear drag, taking down as positive, m dv/dt = mg − bv.

When the object is released from rest, there is no drag yet, so a = g. As it speeds up, drag grows and the net force shrinks, so the acceleration decreases. The speed approaches the terminal speed v_T, at which drag balances gravity and a = 0: mg − bv_T = 0 gives v_T = mg/b for linear drag, and mg = cv_T^2 gives v_T = √(mg/c) for quadratic drag. On a velocity–time graph the curve starts with slope g and levels off toward a horizontal line at v_T. The object never quite reaches v_T, but after a few time constants it is indistinguishable from it.

For linear drag the exact velocity is v(t) = v_T(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with time constant τ = m/b. You do not need to derive this. You can check it by substitution, which needs one new derivative: d/dt e^(kt) = k e^(kt). (A symmetric difference on a calculator confirms it for any value of t.) Then dv/dt = (v_T/τ)e^(−t/τ). Substitute into m dv/dt = mg − bv: the left side is (mv_T/τ)e^(−t/τ), and the right side is mg − bv_T + bv_T e^(−t/τ) = bv_T e^(−t/τ), because mg = bv_T. The two sides agree for every t exactly when τ = m/b, and v(0) = 0 as required. After one time constant v reaches 63% of v_T, and after 3τ it reaches 95%. An object coasting with no other force slows as v = v_0 e^(−t/τ).

Paper investigations in this course use supplied, invented data. They do not replace the hands-on laboratory work, at least 25% of instructional time, that College Board's framework for the AP® Physics C: Mechanics course calls for. Common errors: thinking the drag is zero at terminal speed (it equals the weight); using constant-acceleration equations while drag acts; mixing up τ = m/b with b/m (check the units: τ must be in seconds); and, for an object thrown upward, forgetting that drag points down on the way up, with gravity, and up on the way down.
