items.prompt: The pendulum shown is a uniform 0.60 kg rod 0.80 m long with a uniform 0.40 kg disk of radius 0.10 m centered on its lower end. It swings about a pivot at the rod's top end, perpendicular to the disk's face. Find its rotational inertia about the pivot.
steps: Total: 0.128 + 0.258 = 0.386 kg·m^2. Treating the disk as a particle would give 0.384 kg·m^2, almost the same.
items.skill: Combine parts with the parallel-axis theorem

items.prompt: A uniform disk of radius 0.20 m had a mass of 2.4 kg before a hole of radius 0.050 m was cut through it, centered 0.10 m from the disk's center, as shown. Find the rotational inertia of the remaining piece about the disk's central axis.
steps: The removed piece has mass (2.4 kg)(0.050/0.20)^2 = 0.15 kg.
items.skill: Treat a hole as negative mass

items.prompt: A uniform rod has mass M and length L. What is its rotational inertia about a perpendicular axis located L/4 from one end?
steps: The parallel-axis theorem starts from the center of mass: the axis is L/2 − L/4 = L/4 from the center.
I = ML^2/12 + M(L/4)^2 = 4ML^2/48 + 3ML^2/48 = 7ML^2/48. Adding M(L/4)^2 to the end-axis value ML^2/3 (which gives 19ML^2/48) misuses the theorem.
items.skill: Apply the parallel-axis theorem from the center of mass

items.prompt:
A student measures the rotational inertia of a uniform rod about perpendicular axes at several distances d from its center.
| d (m) | 0 | 0.20 | 0.40 | 0.60 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I (kg·m^2) | 0.30 | 0.42 | 0.78 | 1.38 |
Show that the data fit I = I_cm + Md^2, and find the rod's mass and length.
steps: I − I_cm = 0.12, 0.48 and 1.08 kg·m^2 at d^2 = 0.04, 0.16 and 0.36 m^2: each ratio is 3.0 kg, so I − I_cm is proportional to d^2 with M = 3.0 kg.
items.skill: Extract mass and length from inertia data

items.prompt: A thin disk of mass 5.0 kg and radius 0.40 m is thicker toward its rim: its surface density is σ(r) = kr, where k is a constant. Find k in terms of M and R, show that I = 3MR^2/5 about the central axis, and evaluate I.
steps: Ring elements: dm = σ(r)(2πr dr) = 2πkr^2 dr, so M = ∫ from 0 to R of 2πkr^2 dr = 2πkR^3/3 and k = 3M/(2πR^3).
I = ∫ from 0 to R of r^2(2πkr^2) dr = 2πkR^5/5 = (3M/R^3)(R^5/5) = 3MR^2/5.
I = 0.60(5.0)(0.40)^2 = 0.48 kg·m^2, between a uniform disk (0.40 kg·m^2) and a hoop (0.80 kg·m^2).
items.skill: Integrate a nonuniform disk

items.prompt: A rotating display, shown from above, has a uniform hub disk (4.0 kg, radius 0.20 m) and two flat panels, each 3.0 kg, sticking straight out on opposite sides from r = 0.20 m to r = 1.20 m. Model each panel as a thin uniform rod along the radius. (a) Find the hub's rotational inertia about the vertical central axis. (b) Find one panel's rotational inertia about that axis. (c) Find the total and the fraction contributed by the panels. (d) The designer proposes hinging the panels so they fold to stand vertically at the hub's edge during transport. Explain how this changes the rotational inertia.

rubric.criterion: Finds the hub's I = ½(4.0)(0.20)^2 = 0.080 kg·m^2.
Uses the panel's own center, 0.70 m from the axis, with I_cm = (1/12)(3.0)(1.0)^2 = 0.25 kg·m^2.
Finds one panel's I = 0.25 + (3.0)(0.70)^2 = 1.72 kg·m^2 (or integrates λr^2 from 0.20 to 1.20 m).
Finds the total 3.5 kg·m^2 (3.52 kg·m^2) and the panels' share, about 98%.
Explains that folded panels have all their mass at about 0.20 m from the axis, so their inertia drops to about 2(3.0)(0.20)^2 = 0.24 kg·m^2 and the total to about 0.32 kg·m^2.

items.answer: (a) 0.080 kg·m^2. (b) 1.72 kg·m^2. (c) 3.52 kg·m^2, about 98% from the panels. (d) Folded upright at the hub's edge, each panel's mass sits about 0.20 m from the axis, so the panels contribute only about 0.24 kg·m^2 and the total falls to about 0.32 kg·m^2, roughly a tenth as much.
steps: Panel by integration: λ = 3.0 kg/m, ∫ from 0.20 to 1.20 of 3.0r^2 dr = 1.0(1.728 − 0.008) = 1.72 kg·m^2, matching the parallel-axis result.
items.skill: Model a real object as simple parts

weeks.title: Rotational equilibrium
weeks.objective: Apply the two conditions for equilibrium of an extended body, zero net force and zero net torque about any point, to beams, struts, ladders, limbs and tipping objects, and use Newton's first law in rotational form to explain rotation at constant angular velocity.

connection.before: Week 7's translational equilibrium by components, Week 9's static friction, Week 20's torque, and Week 6's center of mass.
connection.after: Week 23 lets the net torque be nonzero: Newton's second law in rotational form, Στ = Iα, and the Unit 5 test.

days: Newton's first law in rotational form: zero net torque means constant angular velocity; the two equilibrium conditions for an extended body.
Beams and planks on supports: choosing the pivot at an unknown force, center of gravity, and the onset of tipping.
Hinges, struts and cables: two-dimensional forces at a hinge and tension at an angle.
Ladders, limbs and tipping objects: friction limits, muscle forces and the tip-or-slide question.
Mixed practice and a short check on rotational equilibrium.
explanation: Newton's first law has a rotational form: if the net torque on a body about an axis is zero, its angular velocity about that axis does not change. A body at rest stays at rest, and a frictionless wheel spinning at 30 rad/s keeps spinning at 30 rad/s. An extended body is in static equilibrium when it neither accelerates nor starts to rotate, which takes two conditions: the net force is zero, ΣF = 0, and the net torque is zero, Στ = 0. When the net force is zero, the net torque is the same about every point, so if it is zero about one point it is zero about all of them. That freedom is the main tool of the topic.

Choose the point for the torque equation to eliminate unknowns: a force acting at the chosen point has no lever arm and drops out. To find one support force on a plank resting on two supports, take torques about the other support. The weight of a body acts, for torque purposes, at its center of mass (Week 20), so a uniform beam's weight acts at its middle. A hinge can push in any direction in the plane, so give it two unknown components, H_x and H_y; a light cable can only pull along its own length. A typical problem has three unknowns and three equations: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0 and Στ = 0 about a well-chosen point.

Tipping is an equilibrium question at a boundary. As a person walks out past a plank's support, the force from the far support shrinks; the plank is about to tip when that force reaches zero, and from then on the near support is a pivot. A box tips about its lower edge when the line of action of its weight passes outside its base. Comparing the angle at which an object would tip with the angle at which it would slide (tan θ = μ_s) tells which happens first. For a ladder against a frictionless wall, the wall can push only horizontally, so floor friction alone must balance the wall's push, and the friction needed grows as a climber goes higher.

Common errors: writing a torque equation about one point for some forces and another point for the rest; drawing a hinge force straight up when it can have a horizontal part; putting a uniform body's weight at the pivot or at its end instead of at its center; forgetting the body's own weight; and assuming static friction equals μ_sN when the equilibrium needs less. Always check the answer with a second torque equation about a different point.

examples.prompt: A uniform 20 kg plank 4.0 m long rests on supports at 0.50 m and 3.0 m from its left end. A 60 kg person stands 3.2 m from the left end, as shown. Find the force from each support. How far from the left end can the person walk before the plank starts to tip?
examples.answer: Left support 31 N, right support 753 N (7.5 × 10^2 N), both upward. The plank tips when the person passes 3.3 m (3.33 m) from the left end.
steps: Torques about the left support (counterclockwise positive): N_R(2.5 m) − (196 N)(1.5 m) − (588 N)(2.7 m) = 0, so N_R = (294 + 1587.6)/2.5 = 753 N.
Vertical forces: N_L = 196 + 588 − 753 = 31 N.
On the verge of tipping, N_L = 0 and the right support is the pivot: the plank's weight, 1.0 m left of it, balances the person a distance d to its right: (196)(1.0) = (588)d, so d = 0.33 m.
The person can reach 3.0 + 0.33 = 3.33 m; check: at 3.2 m, N_L is small and positive, as found.

examples.prompt: A uniform 8.0 kg strut 1.8 m long is hinged to a wall and held horizontal by a cable from its far end to the wall, at 35° to the strut. A 15 kg sign hangs from the strut 1.5 m from the wall. Find the cable tension and the hinge force.
examples.answer: T = 2.8 × 10^2 N (282 N). Hinge: 231 N horizontally away from the wall and 64 N upward (about 240 N at 15° above the horizontal).
steps: Torques about the hinge remove the hinge force: T sin 35°(1.8 m) = (78.4 N)(0.90 m) + (147 N)(1.5 m) = 70.6 + 220.5 = 291 N·m.
Horizontal: H_x = T cos 35° = 231 N, pushing away from the wall. Vertical: H_y = 78.4 + 147 − T sin 35° = 225.4 − 161.7 = 64 N, upward.
Check with torques about the cable's attachment point: H_y(1.8) − (78.4)(0.90) − (147)(0.30) = 115 − 70.6 − 44.1 ≈ 0.

examples.prompt: A uniform 12 kg ladder 5.0 m long leans against a smooth (frictionless) wall at 60° to the floor, as shown. Find the wall's push, the floor's normal force and friction, and the smallest coefficient of static friction that keeps the ladder in place.
examples.answer: Wall: 34 N; floor: normal force 118 N up and friction 34 N toward the wall; μ_s ≥ 0.29.
steps: The smooth wall pushes only horizontally, N_w. Torques about the foot: N_w(5.0 sin 60°) = (117.6 N)(2.5 cos 60°).
Horizontal: friction f = N_w = 33.9 N, toward the wall. Vertical: N_floor = 117.6 N.

worksheets.title: Balancing torques
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Take counterclockwise as the positive sense of rotation unless a problem says otherwise. Angular quantities are in radians (rad, rad/s, rad/s^2); geometric angles are in degrees. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 30 kg child sits 1.6 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 40 kg child sit, on the other side, to balance it? Ignore the seesaw's own weight, which acts at the pivot.
items.answer: (A) 1.2 m from the pivot
steps: Balance: (30 kg)g(1.6 m) = (40 kg)g d.
d = 48/40 = 1.2 m; the heavier child sits closer.
items.skill: Balance two torques

items.prompt: A uniform 0.15 kg meter stick is balanced on a knife edge at its 40 cm mark. A 0.20 kg mass hangs at the 10 cm mark. Where must a 0.10 kg mass hang to keep the stick level?
items.answer: At the 85 cm mark.
steps: Torques about the knife edge (distances in cm): the 0.20 kg mass, 30 cm left, gives 6.0 (kg·cm)g counterclockwise; the stick's weight at 50 cm, 10 cm right, gives 1.5 (kg·cm)g clockwise.
The 0.10 kg mass must supply the remaining 4.5 (kg·cm)g clockwise: d = 4.5/0.10 = 45 cm right of the edge, at the 85 cm mark.
items.skill: Include a body's own weight in torque balance

items.prompt: A uniform 150 kg beam 6.0 m long rests on supports at its two ends. A 400 kg crate sits 1.5 m from the left end. Find the force from each support.
items.answer: Left support 3.7 × 10^3 N (3675 N); right support 1.7 × 10^3 N (1715 N).
steps: Vertical: N_L = 1470 + 3920 − 1715 = 3675 N; the crate's nearness puts most of the load on the left.
items.skill: Find support forces

items.prompt: A rigid body is in static equilibrium. Which statement must be true?
choices: All the forces on it act at the same point.
The net torque on it is zero only about its center of mass.
The net torque on it is zero about every point.
Each force on it produces zero torque.
items.answer: (C) The net torque on it is zero about every point.
steps: Equilibrium requires ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.
When ΣF = 0, the net torque is the same about every point, so it is zero about all of them; individual forces may have torques that cancel.
items.skill: State the conditions for equilibrium

items.prompt: A mobile hangs from a string tied to a light rod 0.60 m long, with a 0.12 kg ornament at the left end and a 0.20 kg ornament at the right end. How far from the left end must the string be tied for the rod to hang level, and what is the string's tension?
items.answer: 0.38 m (0.375 m) from the left end; tension 3.1 N.
steps: Torques about the string: (0.12)g d = (0.20)g(0.60 − d), so d = 0.12/0.32 = 0.375 m.
Vertical: T = (0.32 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 3.1 N.
items.skill: Locate a balance point

items.prompt: A grinding wheel of radius 0.10 m turns at a steady 30 rad/s. Its motor exerts a torque of 4.0 N·m on it while a tool pressed against the rim exerts a friction force there. The bearings are frictionless. (a) Find the friction force from the tool. (b) A student says, "The wheel is turning, so the torques on it cannot be balanced." Use Newton's first law in rotational form to respond.

rubric.criterion: Recognizes that constant angular velocity means zero net torque.
Explains that zero net torque means no change in ω, not zero ω: the wheel keeps turning at 30 rad/s, just as a body with zero net force keeps a constant velocity.

items.answer: (a) 40 N. (b) Balanced torques mean the angular velocity does not change, not that the wheel is at rest. The motor's 4.0 N·m and the tool's 4.0 N·m cancel, so the wheel keeps turning at a steady 30 rad/s.
steps: Constant ω means α = 0, so Στ = 0: τ_motor = f r.
items.skill: Apply the rotational first law

worksheets.title: Hinges, cables, ladders and limbs
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Take counterclockwise as the positive sense of rotation unless a problem says otherwise. Angular quantities are in radians (rad, rad/s, rad/s^2); geometric angles are in degrees. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A uniform 10 kg beam 2.0 m long is hinged to a wall and held horizontal by a cable from its far end to a point on the wall 1.5 m above the hinge. Find the cable tension and the components of the hinge force.
items.answer: T = 82 N (81.7 N); hinge: 65 N away from the wall and 49 N upward.
steps: The cable rises 1.5 m over 2.0 m, so it is 2.5 m long and makes an angle with sin = 0.60 and cos = 0.80 with the beam.
Torques about the hinge: T(0.60)(2.0 m) = (98 N)(1.0 m), so T = 81.7 N.
H_x = T(0.80) = 65.3 N away from the wall; H_y = 98 − T(0.60) = 98 − 49 = 49 N upward.
items.skill: Solve a hinge-and-cable problem

items.prompt: A uniform 60 kg crate is 1.2 m tall and 0.80 m wide. A worker pushes horizontally on the middle of its top edge. If the crate does not slide, what push makes it start to tip? What is the least coefficient of static friction for which it tips instead of sliding?
steps: At the verge of tipping, the floor's forces act at the far bottom edge. Torques about that edge: F(1.2 m) = (588 N)(0.40 m), so F = 196 N.
Not sliding needs friction 196 N ≤ μ_s(588 N), so μ_s ≥ 0.33.
items.skill: Decide between tipping and sliding

items.prompt: A crate slides slowly along a uniform beam supported at its two ends, moving from the left support toward the right support. How does the force from the left support change?
choices: It stays the same, because the total weight does not change.
It decreases steadily, in proportion to the crate's distance from the left end.
items.answer: (B) It decreases steadily, in proportion to the crate's distance from the left end.
steps: Torques about the right support: N_L L = W_beam(L/2) + W_crate(L − x).
N_L = W_beam/2 + W_crate(1 − x/L), which falls linearly as x grows.
items.skill: Reason about changing support forces

items.prompt: A person holds a 3.0 kg ball with the forearm horizontal, as shown. The 1.5 kg forearm's center of mass is 0.15 m from the elbow, the ball is 0.35 m from the elbow, and the biceps pulls straight up 0.040 m from the elbow. Find the biceps force and the force the upper arm exerts on the forearm at the elbow.
items.answer: Biceps 3.1 × 10^2 N (312 N), up; elbow force 2.7 × 10^2 N (268 N), down.
steps: Vertical: F_elbow = 312 − 14.7 − 29.4 = 268 N, pushing down on the forearm. The short lever arm forces the muscle to pull about 10 times the ball's weight.
items.skill: Analyze a lever in the body

items.prompt: A uniform 20 kg door 0.80 m wide hangs on two hinges 1.6 m apart on its left edge. The upper hinge carries no vertical force. Find the horizontal force each hinge exerts on the door.
items.answer: Each hinge exerts 49 N horizontally, in opposite directions: the upper hinge pulls the door's hinged edge toward the hinge line, and the lower hinge pushes it away.
steps: The weight (196 N) acts 0.40 m from the hinge line. Torques about the lower hinge: H_upper(1.6 m) = (196 N)(0.40 m), so H_upper = 49 N.

Horizontal balance: the lower hinge's horizontal force is 49 N in the opposite direction. The upper hinge must pull because the door's weight tends to swing the top of its hinged edge away from the hinges.
items.skill: Find hinge forces from torques

items.prompt: A uniform 15 kg ladder 4.0 m long leans against a smooth wall at 65° to the floor. The coefficient of static friction between the ladder and the floor is 0.40. A 70 kg painter climbs it. (a) Find the friction force needed when the painter is 3.0 m up the ladder (measured along it). (b) Is the ladder safe there? (c) How far along the ladder can the painter climb before it slips?

rubric.criterion: Takes torques about the foot: N_w(4.0 sin 65°) = [(147)(2.0) + (686)(3.0)] cos 65°.
Finds f = N_w = 274 N (accept 270–280 N).
Compares with μ_sN = 0.40(833 N) = 333 N and concludes the ladder holds.
Sets N_w = 333 N and solves for 3.7 m (accept 3.7–3.8 m) along the ladder, short of the top.

items.answer: (a) 274 N. (b) Yes: the floor can supply up to 0.40 × 833 N = 333 N. (c) About 3.7 m along the ladder; climbing higher makes it slip.
items.skill: Find the friction limit on a ladder

worksheets.title: Equilibrium in context
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Take counterclockwise as the positive sense of rotation unless a problem says otherwise. Angular quantities are in radians (rad, rad/s, rad/s^2); geometric angles are in degrees. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: In the crane shown, the uniform 50 kg boom is 3.0 m long, hinged at its base and tilted 40° above the horizontal. A horizontal cable holds its top, where a 200 kg load hangs. Find the cable tension and the magnitude and direction of the hinge force.
items.answer: T = 2.6 × 10^3 N (2630 N); hinge 3.6 × 10^3 N (3590 N) at 43° above the horizontal, pointing up and away from the mast.
steps: Torques about the hinge: the cable's lever arm is 3.0 sin 40° = 1.93 m; the weights' lever arms are 1.5 cos 40° = 1.15 m and 3.0 cos 40° = 2.30 m.
Hinge: H_x = 2630 N (away from the mast) and H_y = 490 + 1960 = 2450 N, so |H| = 3590 N at tan^−1(2450/2630) = 43° above the horizontal.
items.skill: Solve a tilted-boom equilibrium

items.prompt: A crate slides along a uniform beam 5.0 m long that rests on supports at its two ends. The graph shows the force from the left support as a function of the crate's distance x from the left end. Find the crate's mass and the beam's mass.
steps: When the crate is over the right support (x = 5.0 m), it adds nothing to the left support, so N_L = ½W_beam = 900 N and W_beam = 1800 N: 184 kg.
At x = 0 the crate sits over the left support: N_L = W_crate + 900 N = 3400 N, so W_crate = 2500 N: 255 kg. The slope, −500 N/m, equals −W_crate/L, which checks.
items.skill: Interpret a support-force graph

items.prompt: A log 4.0 m long lies on the ground. Lifting its left end just off the ground takes an upward force of 300 N; lifting its right end instead takes 500 N. What are the log's weight and the position of its center of gravity?
choices: 800 N, 2.0 m from the left end
800 N, 1.5 m from the left end
400 N, 2.0 m from the left end
800 N, 2.5 m from the left end
items.answer: (D) 800 N, 2.5 m from the left end
steps: Lifting the right end, torques about the left end: (500 N)(4.0 m) = W x_cg; lifting the left end, torques about the right end: (300 N)(4.0 m) = W(4.0 − x_cg).
Adding gives W(4.0 m) = 3200 N·m, so W = 800 N and x_cg = 2000/800 = 2.5 m: the heavier end needs the larger lift.
items.skill: Locate a center of gravity from two lifts

items.prompt: A uniform box 0.60 m tall with a square base 0.25 m wide sits on a board that is slowly tilted. The coefficient of static friction is 0.35. At what angle would the box tip over if it could not slide, and at what angle would it slide if it could not tip? Which happens first?
items.answer: Tips at 23° (22.6°); slides at 19° (19.3°); it slides first.
steps: The box tips when the weight's line of action passes the lower edge: tan θ = (width/2)/(height/2) = 0.25/0.60, so θ = 22.6°.
It slides when tan θ = μ_s = 0.35, at θ = 19.3°, which is reached first as the board tilts.
items.skill: Compare tipping and sliding thresholds

items.prompt: A wind turbine's rotor turns at a constant 2.1 rad/s. The wind exerts a torque of 3.6 × 10^5 N·m on it, and bearing friction exerts 0.20 × 10^5 N·m opposing the rotation. What torque does the generator exert? What happens just after the generator is suddenly disconnected?
items.answer: 3.4 × 10^5 N·m opposing the rotation. Once disconnected, the net torque is about 3.4 × 10^5 N·m in the direction of rotation, so the rotor's angular velocity starts to increase.
steps: Constant angular velocity means zero net torque: 3.6 × 10^5 − 0.20 × 10^5 − τ_gen = 0.
τ_gen = 3.4 × 10^5 N·m. Without it the torques no longer cancel, so the rotor speeds up.
items.skill: Use the rotational first law in context

items.prompt: A uniform 30 kg beam 2.4 m long is hinged to a wall at its left end. A cable attached 1.8 m from the wall runs up and back toward the wall at 50° above the beam, and a 25 kg box hangs from the beam's free end, as shown. The beam is horizontal. (a) Draw a force diagram for the beam, showing where each force acts. (b) Find the cable tension. (c) Find the horizontal and vertical components of the hinge force. (d) Would the tension be smaller if the cable were attached at the free end, still at 50°? Justify with a calculation.

rubric.criterion: Draws the hinge force (two components) at the wall, the beam's weight at 1.2 m, the tension at 1.8 m along the cable and the box's weight at 2.4 m.
Writes torques about the hinge: T sin 50°(1.8) = (294)(1.2) + (245)(2.4).
Finds T = 682 N (accept 680–685 N).
Finds H_x = T cos 50° = 439 N away from the wall and H_y = 539 − T sin 50° = 16 N upward (accept 15–17 N).
Finds T = 941/(2.4 × 0.766) = 512 N at the free end and concludes it is smaller because the cable's lever arm is longer.

items.answer: (b) T = 682 N. (c) H_x = 439 N, pushing away from the wall; H_y = 16 N, upward. (d) Yes: attached at the end, T = 941 N·m/(2.4 m × sin 50°) = 512 N, because the same torque is supplied with a longer lever arm.
steps: Horizontal: the cable pulls toward the wall with T cos 50° = 439 N, so the hinge pushes outward with 439 N. Vertical: 539 N − 522.7 N = 16 N.
items.skill: Represent and solve a hinged-beam equilibrium

weeks.title: Newton's second law in rotational form
weeks.objective: Apply Στ = Iα to rigid bodies turning about a fixed axis, link rotating and translating parts of a system through a = αR, integrate time-varying torques for ω(t), and determine a rotational inertia and a friction torque from supplied angular-acceleration data.

connection.before: Week 19's angular kinematics, Week 20's torque, Week 21's rotational inertia, Week 22's equilibrium, and Week 8's connected-body systems.
connection.after: Unit 6 begins in Week 24 with rotational kinetic energy and the work done by a torque, which give a second route to the results of this week.

days: Deriving Στ = Iα from Newton's second law for each particle; first problems with a fixed axis.
Connected systems: hanging blocks, strings and massive pulleys, with a = αR and different tensions on each side.
Torques that change: integrating α(t) = τ(t)/I for ω(t), and a pivoted rod released from rest.
Paper investigation with supplied data: linearizing torque against angular acceleration.
Unit 5 review and the Unit 5 test.
explanation: Newton's second law for rotation follows from the second law for each particle of a rigid body. A particle of mass m_i at distance r_i from a fixed axis has tangential acceleration a_t = r_iα, so the tangential force on it is m_ir_iα and its torque about the axis is m_ir_i^2α. Adding over the body, internal torques cancel in pairs and Στ_ext = (Σm_ir_i^2)α = Iα. The law holds about a fixed axis, and also about an axis through the center of mass even when that axis moves. Torque plays the role of force, rotational inertia the role of mass and angular acceleration the role of acceleration: the same net torque gives a body with four times the rotational inertia a quarter of the angular acceleration.

Most problems join rotating and translating parts. Draw a separate force diagram for each body, write ΣF = ma for each block and Στ = Iα for each wheel, and connect them with the no-slip condition a = αR for a string on a drum of radius R. Because a pulley with rotational inertia needs a net torque to speed up, the string tensions on its two sides differ: (T_1 − T_2)R = Iα. A block of mass m hanging from a string wound on a wheel of inertia I = βMR^2 accelerates at a = mg/(m + βM), less than g because the string's tension both slows the block and spins the wheel. When a torque changes with time, α(t) = τ(t)/I, and ω(t) comes from integrating α(t), just as v(t) came from integrating a(t) in Unit 1.

A rod pivoted at one end shows how rotation differs from free fall. Released from horizontal, a uniform rod of length L feels a gravitational torque Mg(L/2) about the pivot, and I = ML^2/3, so α = 3g/(2L). Its free end starts with tangential acceleration αL = 3g/2, faster than a freely falling object, so a coin resting on the end is left behind. This week's paper investigation uses supplied, invented data on a platform spun by a falling mass. It does not replace the hands-on laboratory work, at least 25% of instructional time, that College Board's framework for the AP® Physics C: Mechanics course calls for, and it does not count toward the AP Course Audit or college lab credit.

Common errors: setting the tension in a string equal to the hanging block's weight when the block accelerates; using one tension on both sides of a massive pulley; taking torques about one point and the rotational inertia about another; mixing the signs of a and α so that a block falls while its drum 'turns backward'; and using constant-α relations when the torque changes with time.

examples.prompt: A 1.5 kg block hangs from a light string wound around a uniform 4.0 kg disk of radius 0.20 m that turns freely on a fixed horizontal axle, as shown. The block is released from rest. Find the block's acceleration, the string's tension and the disk's angular acceleration.
examples.answer: a = 4.2 m/s^2 downward; T = 8.4 N; α = 21 rad/s^2.
steps: Block (down positive): mg − T = ma. Disk: TR = Iα = (½MR^2)(a/R), so T = ½Ma.
T = ½(4.0)(4.2) = 8.4 N, less than the block's weight of 14.7 N, as it must be for the block to accelerate down.

examples.prompt: A uniform 2.0 kg rod 1.2 m long is held horizontal, pivoted at one end, and released, as shown. Find its angular acceleration and the acceleration of its free end just after release.
examples.answer: α = 12 rad/s^2 (12.3 rad/s^2); the free end accelerates at 15 m/s^2 (14.7 m/s^2), which is 1.5g.
steps: Torque of gravity about the pivot: τ = Mg(L/2) = (2.0)(9.8)(0.60) = 11.76 N·m.
Free end: a_t = αL = (12.25)(1.2) = 14.7 m/s^2 = 1.5g. At release ω = 0, so there is no centripetal part.
In symbols α = 3g/(2L) and a_end = 3g/2, independent of the rod's mass.

examples.prompt: A motor applies a torque τ(t) = 0.60t − 0.050t^2 (τ in N·m, t in seconds) to a flywheel with I = 0.25 kg·m^2 that starts from rest on frictionless bearings. Find the flywheel's angular velocity at t = 6.0 s.
examples.answer: 29 rad/s (28.8 rad/s)
steps: ω(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of α dt = 1.2t^2 − 0.0667t^3.

worksheets.title: Torque, inertia and angular acceleration
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Take counterclockwise as the positive sense of rotation unless a problem says otherwise. Angular quantities are in radians (rad, rad/s, rad/s^2); geometric angles are in degrees. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A net torque of 12 N·m acts on a wheel whose rotational inertia about its axle is 3.0 kg·m^2. What is its angular acceleration?
steps: Στ = Iα, so α = Στ/I.
items.skill: Apply Στ = Iα

items.prompt: A flywheel with I = 0.80 kg·m^2 spins at 50 rad/s. A brake pad pressed against it 0.25 m from the axle with a normal force of 60 N brings it to rest; μ_k = 0.50. Find the braking torque, the angular acceleration, the stopping time and the number of revolutions it makes while stopping.
items.answer: Torque 7.5 N·m; α = −9.4 rad/s^2 (−9.375 rad/s^2); 5.3 s (5.33 s); 21 revolutions (133 rad).
steps: Friction f = μ_kN = 0.50(60 N) = 30 N at r = 0.25 m: τ = 7.5 N·m opposing the rotation.
items.skill: Analyze a braking torque

items.prompt: A uniform 12 kg grindstone disk of radius 0.25 m is brought from rest to 90 rad/s in 6.0 s at a steady rate. What net torque does this take? If the bearings exert a friction torque of 1.2 N·m, what torque must the motor supply?
items.answer: Net torque 5.6 N·m (5.63 N·m); motor torque 6.8 N·m (6.83 N·m).
steps: Στ = Iα = (0.375)(15) = 5.63 N·m; the motor must also overcome friction: 5.63 + 1.2 = 6.83 N·m.
items.skill: Find the torque a motor must supply

items.prompt: A wheel with rotational inertia 0.050 kg·m^2 turns freely on an axle of radius 0.030 m. A string wound around the axle holds a 0.40 kg mass, which is released from rest. Find the mass's acceleration, the string's tension and the time the mass takes to fall 1.0 m.
steps: Mass: mg − T = ma. Wheel: Tr = Iα = I(a/r), so T = (I/r^2)a with I/r^2 = 55.6 kg.
t = √(2h/a) = √(2(1.0)/0.070) = 5.34 s. The small axle radius makes the wheel act like a huge effective mass.
items.skill: Analyze a wheel and axle

items.prompt: Two uniform disks have equal masses, but disk Q has twice the radius of disk P. The same tangential force is applied at the rim of each. How does Q's angular acceleration compare with P's?
items.answer: (B) It is half as large.
steps: α = τ/I = FR/(½MR^2) = 2F/(MR).
Doubling R doubles the torque but quadruples I, so α is halved.
items.skill: Reason with proportions in Στ = Iα

items.prompt: A uniform 1.6 kg rod 0.90 m long is held horizontal by a frictionless hinge at one end and released. Just after release, find (a) the rod's angular acceleration, (b) the acceleration of its center of mass, and (c) the force the hinge exerts on the rod.

rubric.criterion: Finds a_cm = α(L/2) = 3g/4 = 7.4 m/s^2 (7.35 m/s^2) downward.
Uses Mg − F_hinge = Ma_cm to get F_hinge = Mg/4 = 3.9 N upward.

items.answer: (a) 16 rad/s^2. (b) 7.4 m/s^2 downward. (c) 3.9 N upward, a quarter of the rod's weight.
items.skill: Combine rotational and translational laws

worksheets.title: Connected systems and changing torques
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Take counterclockwise as the positive sense of rotation unless a problem says otherwise. Angular quantities are in radians (rad, rad/s, rad/s^2); geometric angles are in degrees. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: In the Atwood machine shown, the pulley is a uniform 2.0 kg disk of radius 0.10 m on a frictionless axle, and the string does not slip. The blocks are 3.0 kg and 2.0 kg. Find the blocks' acceleration and the tension on each side of the pulley.
items.answer: a = 1.6 m/s^2 (1.63 m/s^2); 25 N (24.5 N) on the 3.0 kg side and 23 N (22.9 N) on the 2.0 kg side.
steps: Take the 3.0 kg block's downward motion as positive. 3.0 kg: 3.0g − T_1 = 3.0a. 2.0 kg: T_2 − 2.0g = 2.0a. Pulley: (T_1 − T_2)R = (½MR^2)(a/R), so T_1 − T_2 = 1.0a.
T_1 = 3.0(9.8 − 1.63) = 24.5 N and T_2 = 2.0(9.8 + 1.63) = 22.9 N; their difference spins the pulley.
items.skill: Solve an Atwood machine with a massive pulley

items.prompt: In the setup shown, the 4.0 kg block slides on a table with μ_k = 0.20, and the hanging block is 2.0 kg. The pulley has I = 0.020 kg·m^2 and radius 0.10 m. Find the acceleration and both tensions.
items.answer: a = 1.5 m/s^2 (1.47 m/s^2); hanging side 17 N (16.7 N); table side 14 N (13.7 N).
steps: Hanging block: 2.0g − T_h = 2.0a. Table block: T_t − 0.20(4.0)g = 4.0a. Pulley: (T_h − T_t)R = I(a/R), so T_h − T_t = (I/R^2)a = 2.0a.
items.skill: Combine friction, tension and a massive pulley

items.prompt: In an Atwood machine whose pulley has rotational inertia, the heavier block accelerates downward. How do the string tensions on the two sides of the pulley compare?
choices: Both tensions equal the average of the two weights.
The tensions are equal, because it is one string.
The tension is greater on the lighter block's side.
The tension is greater on the heavier block's side.
items.answer: (D) The tension is greater on the heavier block's side.
steps: The pulley's angular acceleration needs a net torque: (T_heavy − T_light)R = Iα > 0.
So the tension on the heavier block's side must be larger; equal tensions hold only for a pulley with negligible inertia.
items.skill: Explain tension differences across a massive pulley

items.prompt: A turntable with I = 0.12 kg·m^2 starts from rest. A motor applies a torque τ(t) = 0.36 − 0.060t (N·m, t in seconds) for 6.0 s, and friction is negligible. Find the turntable's angular velocity and the angle it has turned at t = 6.0 s.
items.answer: ω = 9.0 rad/s; θ = 36 rad.
items.skill: Integrate a time-varying torque

items.prompt: A fan's blades (I = 0.020 kg·m^2) coast after the power is cut, slowed by an air-drag torque τ = −bω with b = 0.0050 N·m·s. (a) Show that ω(t) = ω_0e^(−t/T) satisfies Στ = Iα, and find the time constant T. (b) If ω_0 = 50 rad/s, find ω at t = 6.0 s and the time for ω to fall to half its starting value.
items.answer: (a) T = I/b = 4.0 s. (b) 11 rad/s (11.2 rad/s) at 6.0 s; half speed at 2.8 s (2.77 s).
steps: dω/dt = −(1/T)ω_0e^(−t/T) = −ω/T, so Iα = −(I/T)ω, which equals −bω when T = I/b = 0.020/0.0050 = 4.0 s.
items.skill: Verify an exponential solution for rotation

items.prompt: A uniform rod of length L, pivoted at one end, is released from rest at an angle θ below the horizontal. (a) Show that its angular acceleration at release is α = (3g/(2L)) cos θ. (b) Show that the acceleration of its free end at release does not depend on L or M. (c) Small coins rest on the rod's upper surface at several distances x from the pivot. Just after release, a coin stays in contact only if the rod's surface beneath it does not accelerate away from it faster than gravity can follow. Find the distances x at which the coins lose contact. (d) Explain physically how part of the rod can accelerate faster than gravity alone would accelerate it.

rubric.criterion: Uses τ = Mg(L/2) cos θ and I = ML^2/3 to get α = (3g/(2L)) cos θ.
Finds a_end = αL = (3/2)g cos θ, free of L and M, directed perpendicular to the rod.

Compares the surface's acceleration αx, perpendicular to the rod, with gravity's component perpendicular to the rod, g cos θ, and finds that coins beyond x = 2L/3 lose contact, for any release angle short of vertical.
Explains that the rigid rod turns as one piece, so internal forces slow its inner part and speed up its outer part compared with each piece falling separately.

items.answer: (a) α = Mg(L/2) cos θ / (ML^2/3) = (3g/(2L)) cos θ. (b) a_end = αL = (3/2)g cos θ. (c) At release ω = 0, so the surface at distance x accelerates at αx = (3gx/(2L)) cos θ perpendicular to the rod, while a free coin's acceleration in that direction is g cos θ. The surface pulls away when 3x/(2L) > 1: every coin beyond x = 2L/3 loses contact, whatever the release angle (below vertical). (d) If the pieces of the rod were separate, each would fall with g. Because the rod is rigid, it must turn as a unit with one α, so the inner part, which would fall faster than the rotation allows, pushes the outer part down through the rod's internal forces, and the outer part moves faster than free fall.
steps: At release ω = 0, so each point's acceleration is purely tangential: αx, perpendicular to the rod.
Gravity's component perpendicular to the rod is g cos θ; equality αx = g cos θ gives x = 2L/3.
items.skill: Compare rotational and free-fall accelerations

worksheets.title: Paper investigation: torque and angular acceleration
worksheets.directions:
Paper investigation. This is a paper investigation with supplied, invented data. It does not replace the hands-on laboratory work, at least 25% of instructional time, that College Board's framework for the AP® Physics C: Mechanics course calls for, and it does not count toward the AP Course Audit or college lab credit. A horizontal platform turns on a vertical axle, as shown. A thread wound around a spool of radius r = 0.025 m on the axle runs over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging mass m. Each mass is released from rest 0.80 m above the floor, and the time t to reach the floor is recorded. The model is τ_thread − τ_f = Iα, where τ_f is a constant friction torque in the axle. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.
| m (kg) | 0.020 | 0.040 | 0.060 | 0.080 | 0.100 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| t (s) | 10.52 | 6.85 | 5.39 | 4.64 | 4.10 |

items.prompt: For each trial, find the hanging mass's acceleration a (assumed constant) and the platform's angular acceleration α.
steps: The thread unwinds from the spool without slipping, so α = a/r = a/0.025 m, for example 0.0145/0.025 = 0.578 rad/s^2.
items.skill: Process timing data into accelerations

items.prompt: The thread's torque on the platform is τ = T r, where T = m(g − a) is the thread's tension. Compute τ for each trial. Then plot τ against α on the grid provided, label and scale both axes, and draw a best-fit straight line.

rubric.criterion: Computes τ = 4.89, 9.77, 14.6, 19.5 and 24.3 (all × 10^−3 N·m), ±1 in the last digit.
Labels both axes with quantities and units and chooses scales that spread the points over the grid.
Plots all five points correctly.
Draws one straight best-fit line with points on both sides that does not pass through the origin.

items.answer: τ = 4.89, 9.77, 14.6, 19.5 and 24.3 × 10^−3 N·m. The points lie close to a straight line that crosses the τ axis above zero.
steps: The model rearranges to τ = Iα + τ_f: a straight line with slope I and vertical intercept τ_f.
items.skill: Plot linearized rotational data

items.prompt: Find the slope and the vertical intercept of your line, with units. What physical quantity does each represent?
items.answer: Slope ≈ 6.0 × 10^−3 kg·m^2 (accept 5.8–6.2 × 10^−3), the platform's rotational inertia I. Intercept ≈ 1.5 × 10^−3 N·m (accept 1.2–1.8 × 10^−3), the axle's friction torque τ_f.
steps: Since τ = Iα + τ_f, the slope is I, and the intercept, the torque needed before any angular acceleration occurs, is the friction torque τ_f ≈ 1.5 × 10^−3 N·m.
items.skill: Interpret slope and intercept

items.prompt: A second student uses τ = mgr, ignoring the hanging mass's acceleration. How does this change the slope of the τ–α graph and the rotational inertia found from it?
choices: The slope is unchanged, because a is the same in both calculations.
The slope is about 1% smaller, so I is slightly underestimated.
The slope is about 1% larger, so I is slightly overestimated.
The slope doubles, because the weight replaces the tension.
items.answer: (C) The slope is about 1% larger, so I is slightly overestimated.
steps: mgr exceeds the true torque by mar, which grows with the mass and the acceleration, so the larger-α points are raised most.
For the last trial, mar = (0.100)(0.0952)(0.025) = 2.4 × 10^−4 N·m out of 0.0243 N·m, about 1%, so the slope rises by about 1%.
items.skill: Evaluate an approximation

items.prompt: The times were measured with a hand-held stopwatch with a reaction-time uncertainty of about 0.2 s. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in a for the trial with the shortest time. Which trials are least reliable, and how could the timing be improved?
items.answer: For t = 4.10 s: about 5% in t and about 10% in a, because a = 2h/t^2. The heaviest-mass (shortest-time) trials are least reliable; a longer drop, a light gate at the floor, or averaging several repeated trials would reduce the uncertainty.
steps: Fractional uncertainty in t: 0.2/4.10 = 0.049, about 5%.
a depends on 1/t^2, so its fractional uncertainty is about twice as large: about 10%. Shorter times have larger fractional uncertainty.
items.skill: Propagate a timing uncertainty

items.prompt: A uniform 1.5 kg disk of radius 0.15 m is placed on the platform, centered on the axle. Using your values of I and τ_f, calculate the expected time for the 0.060 kg mass to fall the 0.80 m.
items.answer: About 11 s (10.5 s).
items.skill: Calculate with a fitted model

items.prompt: Describe how to use this apparatus to test the parallel-axis theorem with the 1.5 kg disk. Include what you would change, what you would measure, the graph you would make and what result would support the theorem.
items.answer: Sample procedure: measure the platform's τ–α line alone (slope I_0). Place the disk with its center on the axle, repeat the set of hanging masses and find the new slope I_1; then move the disk so its center is a measured distance d from the axle (several values, such as 0.05 to 0.20 m) and repeat for each. Plot the slope I (or I − I_0) against d^2. The parallel-axis theorem gives a straight line with slope equal to the disk's mass, 1.5 kg, and intercept I_1 − I_0 ≈ ½MR^2.
steps: For each placement, the inertia comes from the slope of a τ–α graph, so friction is separated out in the intercept.
I = I_0 + ½MR^2 + Md^2 is linear in d^2 with slope M.
items.skill: Design an experimental test

weeks.title: Rotational kinetic energy and work by torque
weeks.objective: Compute the kinetic energy of rigid bodies rotating about a fixed axis, find the work done by constant and varying torques as W = ∫τ dθ, and apply the rotational work–energy theorem and P = τω to wheels, rods and pulley systems.

connection.before: Unit 5 rotational kinematics, torque and rotational inertia (including I by integration and the parallel-axis theorem), and the Unit 3 work–energy theorem with W = ∫F dx.
connection.after: Week 25 introduces angular momentum L = Iω and angular impulse ∫τ dt, the rotational partners of momentum and impulse.

days: Rotational kinetic energy: add ½m_i v_i^2 over a rigid body with v_i = r_iω to get K = ½Iω^2; compare hoops, disks and dumbbells turning at the same rate.
Work done by a torque: dW = τ dθ for a tangential force, constant torques through whole revolutions, and why θ must be in radians.
Varying torques: W = ∫τ dθ as the signed area under a τ–θ graph and by antiderivatives; the angular speed is greatest where the net torque changes sign.
Power P = τω and energy bookkeeping for systems that rotate and translate: hanging blocks on massive pulleys, falling rods and poles.
Mixed practice: choose an axis, write K for every moving part, and check one answer two ways (energy and torque); short check.
explanation: A rigid body turning about a fixed axis with angular speed ω has every particle moving in a circle, with speed v_i = r_iω, where r_i is that particle's distance from the axis. Adding the particles' kinetic energies gives K = Σ½m_i r_i^2 ω^2 = ½Iω^2, where I = Σm_i r_i^2 (or ∫r^2 dm) is the rotational inertia about that axis. Rotational kinetic energy is ordinary kinetic energy of moving mass, measured in joules; the formula just collects it for a body whose parts move at different speeds. Because I depends on how far the mass sits from the axis, a hoop (I = MR^2) turning at the same ω as a solid disk of equal mass and radius (I = ½MR^2) has twice the kinetic energy. Useful results from Unit 5: a thin rod has I = ML^2/12 about its center and ML^2/3 about one end, a solid sphere 2MR^2/5, and a thin spherical shell 2MR^2/3.

A force F applied tangentially at distance r from the axis moves its point of application along an arc ds = r dθ, so it does work dW = Fr dθ = τ dθ. For a varying torque, W = ∫τ dθ from θ_1 to θ_2, which is the signed area under a graph of τ against θ, the rotational partner of W = ∫F dx. The angle must be in radians: then N·m × rad = J, and one revolution is 2π rad. The rotational work–energy theorem follows: the net work done by the torques on a rigid body equals its change in rotational kinetic energy, W_net = ½Iω_2^2 − ½Iω_1^2. Dividing dW = τ dθ by dt gives the power delivered by a torque, P = τω.

To solve an energy problem with rotation, list every moving part and write its kinetic energy: ½Mv^2 for a block, ½Iω^2 for a wheel, and both are linked through v = ωR when a string does not slip on a pulley. A rigid body's gravitational potential energy is Mg times the height of its center of mass, so a uniform rod swinging down from horizontal loses Mg(L/2). When a torque varies with angle, such as gravity's torque Mg(L/2) cos θ on a rod at angle θ below the horizontal, integrate it; the result matches the change in Mgy_cm, which is a good two-way check. When the torque changes sign, the angular speed is largest at the angle where the net torque is zero.

Common errors: using degrees or revolutions in τΔθ or in ½Iω^2 (convert to radians and rad/s); taking I about the wrong axis, for example ML^2/12 for a rod that pivots about its end; forgetting the translational kinetic energy of a hanging block or the rotational energy of a massive pulley; treating a torque that depends on angle as constant; and computing a rod's change in potential energy from its end rather than from its center of mass.

examples.prompt: A flywheel is a uniform solid disk of mass 12 kg and radius 0.25 m spinning at 300 revolutions per minute about its axle. Find its rotational kinetic energy.
steps: Rotational inertia of a solid disk about its axle: I = ½MR^2 = ½(12 kg)(0.25 m)^2 = 0.375 kg·m^2.
Convert the rate to rad/s: ω = (300 rev/min)(2π rad/rev)/(60 s/min) = 31.4 rad/s.

examples.prompt: A motor turns a wheel (I = 0.80 kg·m^2) from rest with a torque that grows with angle, τ(θ) = 4.0 + 0.50θ, in N·m with θ in radians. Ignoring friction, find the work done by the motor during the first 6.0 rad and the wheel's angular speed at θ = 6.0 rad.
examples.answer: W = 33 J; ω = 9.1 rad/s.
steps: The motor's torque is the only torque, so W = ΔK = ½Iω^2 − 0.

examples.prompt: A uniform 2.0 kg rod 1.2 m long is pivoted at one end, as shown, held horizontal and released from rest. Find its angular speed as it swings through the vertical and the speed of its free end then. Check the energy change by integrating gravity's torque.
examples.answer: ω = 4.9 rad/s (4.95 rad/s); the free end moves at 5.9 m/s.
steps: The center of mass falls L/2 = 0.60 m, so ΔU = −Mg(L/2) = −(2.0)(9.8)(0.60) = −11.8 J, and K at the bottom is 11.8 J.
Check: with θ measured down from horizontal, gravity's torque about the pivot is Mg(L/2) cos θ, and ∫ from 0 to π/2 of (11.76 N·m) cos θ dθ = 11.76 [sin θ] from 0 to π/2 = 11.8 J, the same work.

worksheets.title: Rotational kinetic energy and constant torques
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A thin hoop and a uniform solid disk have the same mass and radius and spin about their central axes at the same angular speed. What is the ratio K_hoop/K_disk of their kinetic energies?
steps: K = ½Iω^2 with the same ω, so K_hoop/K_disk = I_hoop/I_disk.
I_hoop/I_disk = MR^2/(½MR^2) = 2: all the hoop's mass is at the rim, where it moves fastest.
items.skill: Compare rotational kinetic energies

items.prompt: A grinding wheel with rotational inertia 0.050 kg·m^2 spins at 3000 revolutions per minute. Find its rotational kinetic energy.
steps: ω = (3000 rev/min)(2π rad/rev)/(60 s/min) = 314 rad/s.
items.skill: Compute K = ½Iω^2 with unit conversion

items.prompt: A constant 12 N·m torque turns a wheel (I = 1.5 kg·m^2) from rest through 5.0 revolutions. Ignoring friction, find the work done by the torque and the wheel's final angular speed.
steps: Δθ = 5.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 31.4 rad, so W = τΔθ = (12 N·m)(31.4 rad) = 377 J.
items.skill: Find work done by a constant torque

items.prompt: A motor exerts a constant 9.0 N·m torque on a flywheel (I = 2.0 kg·m^2) that starts from rest. (a) How long does the flywheel take to reach 150 rad/s? (b) What power does the motor deliver at that moment? (c) What is the average power over the spin-up, and why is it different?
items.answer: (a) 33 s. (b) 1.4 × 10^3 W (1350 W). (c) 675 W (6.8 × 10^2 W): the power P = τω grows in proportion to ω, so its average over a uniform spin-up is half the final value.
steps: The motor does W = ½Iω^2 = ½(2.0)(150)^2 = 2.25 × 10^4 J in 33.3 s, an average of 675 W, half of 1350 W because ω rises linearly from zero.
items.skill: Use P = τω and average power

items.prompt: Two 0.50 kg balls are fixed to the ends of a light rod 0.60 m long. Find the system's kinetic energy when it turns at 8.0 rad/s (a) about an axis through the center of the rod and (b) about an axis through one ball, both axes perpendicular to the rod.
steps: (b) One ball is on the axis and the other 0.60 m away: I = (0.50)(0.60)^2 = 0.18 kg·m^2 and K = ½(0.18)(64) = 5.76 J, double because the same ω moves the far ball twice as fast.
items.skill: Find K for different axes

items.prompt: A spinning wheel has 400 J of kinetic energy. A brake applies a constant 20 N·m friction torque until the wheel stops. Through what angle does the wheel turn while stopping?
items.answer: (B) 20 rad
steps: The brake's work equals the change in kinetic energy: −τΔθ = 0 − 400 J.
Δθ = 400 J/20 N·m = 20 rad; 8000 rad multiplies instead of dividing.
items.skill: Apply the rotational work–energy theorem

worksheets.title: Varying torques and energy with rotation
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: The graph shows the net torque on a wheel (I = 0.30 kg·m^2), starting from rest, as it turns. Find the work done from θ = 0 to θ = 6 rad and the wheel's angular speed at θ = 6 rad.
items.answer: W = 27 J; ω = 13 rad/s (13.4 rad/s).
steps: Work is the area under the τ–θ graph: triangle ½(2)(6) = 6 J, rectangle (3)(6) = 18 J, triangle ½(1)(6) = 3 J, a total of 27 J.
items.skill: Find work as area under a τ–θ graph

items.prompt: The net torque on a turntable (I = 0.50 kg·m^2) that starts from rest is τ(θ) = 3.0θ − 0.50θ^2, in N·m with θ in radians, for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 8.0 rad. (a) At what angle is the angular speed greatest, and what is it? (b) Find the angular speed at θ = 8.0 rad.
items.answer: (a) At θ = 6.0 rad, where the torque changes sign: ω = 8.5 rad/s. (b) 6.5 rad/s.
steps: τ > 0 speeds the turntable up and τ < 0 slows it, so ω peaks where τ = 0: 3.0θ − 0.50θ^2 = 0 at θ = 6.0 rad. W(θ) = 1.5θ^2 − θ^3/6, so W(6.0) = 54 − 36 = 18 J and ω = √(2(18)/0.50) = 8.49 rad/s.
items.skill: Integrate a torque that changes sign

items.prompt: As a wheel (I = 0.20 kg·m^2) turns from rest, its kinetic energy is K = 0.40θ^2, in joules with θ in radians. Find the net torque on it as a function of θ and its value at θ = 5.0 rad, and write the angular speed as a function of θ.
items.answer: τ = dK/dθ = 0.80θ N·m, which is 4.0 N·m at θ = 5.0 rad; ω = 2.0θ rad/s.
steps: By the work–energy theorem K(θ) = ∫τ dθ, so the torque is the slope of K against θ: τ = d(0.40θ^2)/dθ = 0.80θ.
½(0.20)ω^2 = 0.40θ^2 gives ω^2 = 4.0θ^2, so ω = 2.0θ (rad/s with θ in rad).
items.skill: Read torque as the slope of K against θ

items.prompt: A constant 0.60 N·m torque spins a small wheel (I = 0.030 kg·m^2) from rest. Find the power the torque delivers at t = 2.0 s, and find the work done in the first 2.0 s by integrating the power. Check your work against the wheel's kinetic energy.
items.answer: P = 24 W at t = 2.0 s; W = 24 J, which equals K = ½Iω^2 = 24 J.
steps: α = τ/I = 20 rad/s^2, so ω(t) = 20t and P(t) = τω = 12t W; at 2.0 s, P = 24 W.
W = ∫P dt from 0 to 2.0 = [6t^2] from 0 to 2.0 = 24 J; check: ω(2.0) = 40 rad/s and ½(0.030)(40)^2 = 24 J.
items.skill: Integrate power to find work

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg block hangs from a light string wound around a uniform solid disk pulley of mass 4.0 kg and radius 0.10 m, as shown, which turns without friction. The block is released from rest. Find its speed after it falls 1.5 m, and the fraction of the energy released that goes into turning the pulley.
items.answer: 3.8 m/s; one half of the energy goes to the pulley.
steps: mgh = ½mv^2 + ½Iω^2 with ω = v/R and I = ½MR^2, so mgh = ½(m + M/2)v^2.
items.skill: Share energy between translation and rotation

items.prompt: A uniform 3.0 kg pole 2.0 m long is hinged to the ground at its lower end and is released from rest leaning 30° from the vertical, as shown. Measure θ from the vertical. (a) Write gravity's torque about the hinge as a function of θ. (b) Integrate it to find the work gravity does as the pole falls flat. (c) Find the pole's angular speed and the speed of its top just before it hits the ground. (d) A stone dropped from the height where the pole's top started would land at 5.8 m/s. Explain why the top of the pole lands faster.

rubric.criterion: (a) τ = Mg(L/2) sin θ = (29.4 N·m) sin θ.
(b) W = ∫ from π/6 to π/2 of 29.4 sin θ dθ = 29.4 cos(π/6) = 25 J (accept 25–26 J).
(c) Uses I = ML^2/3 = 4.0 kg·m^2 and W = ½Iω^2 to get ω = 3.6 rad/s.
(c) Top speed v = ωL = 7.1 m/s (accept 7.0–7.2 m/s).

(d) Explains that the pole's energy comes from its center of mass falling, and in a rotating rod the top moves fastest, so the top reaches a speed greater than free fall from its height (the rod's lower parts pull the top along faster).

items.answer: (a) τ = 29.4 sin θ N·m. (b) 25 J. (c) ω = 3.6 rad/s; the top moves at 7.1 m/s. (d) The energy released depends on the drop of the center of mass, but the rotational speed is shared so the top, farthest from the hinge, moves faster than a freely falling stone.
steps: The weight acts at the center, L/2 = 1.0 m from the hinge, with lever arm (L/2) sin θ, so τ = (3.0)(9.8)(1.0) sin θ.
W = 29.4[−cos θ] from π/6 to π/2 = 29.4(0.866 − 0) = 25.5 J, equal to Mg times the 0.866 m drop of the center of mass.

ω = √(2(25.5)/4.0) = 3.57 rad/s and v_top = (3.57)(2.0) = 7.1 m/s, larger than √(2g(1.73 m)) = 5.8 m/s: ½(ML^2/3)ω^2 = Mg(drop of the center) gives v_top^2 = 3g(drop of the top), 1.5 times the free-fall value 2g(drop of the top).
items.skill: Integrate a torque that varies with angle

worksheets.title: Energy in rotating systems
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: Blocks of 3.0 kg and 1.0 kg hang from a light string over a pulley with rotational inertia 0.020 kg·m^2 and radius 0.10 m, as shown. The string does not slip and the axle is frictionless. Released from rest, how fast are the blocks moving after the 3.0 kg block has fallen 0.80 m?
steps: Potential energy released: (3.0 − 1.0)(9.8)(0.80) = 15.7 J.
items.skill: Apply energy conservation to a massive pulley

items.prompt: An energy-storage flywheel is a uniform 50 kg solid cylinder of radius 0.40 m. For safety the speed of its rim must not exceed 200 m/s. How much energy can it store, and for how long could it supply 2.0 kW?
steps: ω = v_rim/R = 500 rad/s and I = ½MR^2 = 4.0 kg·m^2, so K = ½(4.0)(500)^2 = 5.0 × 10^5 J (equivalently ¼Mv_rim^2).
items.skill: Apply rotational energy to a design limit

items.prompt: The same constant torque is applied to two wheels, starting from rest, through the same angle. Wheel 2 has twice the rotational inertia of wheel 1. Which statement about the wheels afterward is correct?
choices: Wheel 1 has twice the kinetic energy of wheel 2.
Both wheels have the same kinetic energy, and wheel 1 spins √2 times as fast.
Both wheels have the same angular speed.
Wheel 2 has twice the kinetic energy of wheel 1.
items.answer: (B) Both wheels have the same kinetic energy, and wheel 1 spins √2 times as fast.
steps: Each wheel receives the same work, W = τΔθ, so each gains the same kinetic energy.
items.skill: Reason from equal work

items.prompt: A rope wound around a reel (a uniform 2.0 kg solid disk of radius 0.20 m on a frictionless axle) is pulled with a constant 15 N force until 3.0 m of rope has unwound. Find the work done in two ways, as force times distance and as torque times angle, then find the reel's final angular speed and the rope's speed.
items.answer: W = 45 J both ways; ω = 47 rad/s; the rope moves at 9.5 m/s.
steps: Force × distance: (15 N)(3.0 m) = 45 J. Torque × angle: τ = (15)(0.20) = 3.0 N·m and Δθ = 3.0/0.20 = 15 rad, so W = 45 J.
items.skill: Connect work by a force and work by a torque

items.prompt: A lathe motor keeps a chuck (I = 0.015 kg·m^2) turning at a steady 120 rad/s against a friction torque of 0.35 N·m. (a) What power does the motor supply? (b) When the motor is switched off, how many revolutions does the chuck make before it stops, and how long does that take?
items.answer: (a) 42 W. (b) About 49 revolutions (309 rad), in 5.1 s.
steps: At steady speed the motor's torque balances friction, so P = τω = (0.35)(120) = 42 W.
items.skill: Use power and energy for friction torques

items.prompt: Rod A is a uniform rod of mass M and length L. Rod B has the same length and mass, but its rod is light and its mass M is a small ball at its free end. Each is pivoted at one end and released from rest horizontal. (a) Without calculating, decide which rod has the larger angular speed at the vertical, and explain. (b) Derive ω at the vertical for each rod in terms of g and L. (c) Show that your results support your choice.

rubric.criterion: (a) Chooses rod A, reasoning that A loses less potential energy (its center falls L/2) but its rotational inertia is much smaller (ML^2/3 versus ML^2), so less energy is needed per unit ω^2.
(b) Rod A: MgL/2 = ½(ML^2/3)ω^2, so ω_A = √(3g/L).
(b) Rod B: MgL = ½(ML^2)ω^2, so ω_B = √(2g/L).
(c) Notes √(3g/L) > √(2g/L), consistent with the choice in (a).

items.answer: (a) Rod A. (b) ω_A = √(3g/L); ω_B = √(2g/L). (c) 3 > 2, so rod A turns faster.
steps: Rod A releases half the potential energy of rod B but has one third of its rotational inertia.
ω^2 = 2ΔU/I: A gives 2(MgL/2)/(ML^2/3) = 3g/L and B gives 2MgL/ML^2 = 2g/L.
items.skill: Compare rotating bodies with energy

weeks.title: Angular momentum and its conservation
weeks.objective: Find the angular momentum of particles and rigid bodies about a chosen point, relate its change to angular impulse ∫τ dt, and apply conservation of angular momentum to changing shapes, coupled rotors and collisions with pivoted or free rods.

connection.before: Week 24 rotational kinetic energy, the Unit 4 impulse–momentum theorem and momentum conservation, and the Unit 5 cross product τ = r × F.
connection.after: Week 26 combines translation and rotation in rolling, where angular momentum about the contact point and static friction both matter.

days: Angular momentum of a particle, L = r × p, with the moment arm r⊥; why a particle moving in a straight line has constant L about any point.
Rigid bodies: L = Iω about a fixed axis; τ_net = dL/dt and angular impulse ΔL = ∫τ dt as the area under a τ–t graph.
Conservation: zero net external torque about a point; skaters, collapsing stars, coupled disks and the energy change when I changes.
Collisions with rotating objects: a pivot's force has no torque about the pivot, so conserve L about it; free rods conserve both p and L.
Mixed practice with graphs, vectors and collisions; short check.
explanation: The angular momentum of a particle about a point O is L = r × p, where r runs from O to the particle and p = mv. In a plane its magnitude is L = mvr⊥, where r⊥ is the moment arm: the perpendicular distance from O to the line along which the particle moves. Take counterclockwise as positive, or use the right-hand rule for direction. A particle moving in a straight line at constant velocity has the same r⊥ at every instant, so its angular momentum about any point stays constant even though r changes. For a rigid body turning about a fixed axis, adding m_i r_i^2 ω over the particles gives L = Iω, measured in kg·m^2/s.

Differentiating L = r × p gives dL/dt = r × F = τ, so the net external torque about a point equals the rate of change of angular momentum about that point: τ_net = dL/dt. Over a time interval, the angular impulse ∫τ dt equals ΔL, which is the signed area under a graph of torque against time. This is the rotational partner of J = ∫F dt = Δp, and it is the right tool when a torque acts for a known time, while W = ∫τ dθ (week 24) is the tool when it acts through a known angle.

When the net external torque on a system about a point is zero, the system's angular momentum about that point is conserved: I_1ω_1 = I_2ω_2 for a body that changes shape, and the total of every part's L for several bodies. Kinetic energy need not be conserved. Writing K = L^2/(2I) shows that pulling mass inward (smaller I at the same L) increases K; the person or motor doing the pulling does that work. In a collision with a pivoted object, the pivot pushes on the object, so linear momentum is not conserved, but the pivot force acts at the pivot and has zero torque about it, so angular momentum about the pivot is conserved. For an object free to move, such as a rod on ice, both the linear momentum and the angular momentum about any fixed point are conserved.

Common errors: conserving linear momentum in a collision with a pivoted body; leaving out the incoming particle's angular momentum mvr⊥; using the distance r instead of the moment arm r⊥; assuming kinetic energy is conserved whenever angular momentum is; and adding angular momenta that turn in opposite senses without signs.
