items.prompt: The bob of a simple pendulum is replaced by one with twice the mass, at the same distance from the pivot. What happens to the period of small oscillations?
choices: It decreases by a factor of √2.
It increases by a factor of √2.
items.answer: (B) It is unchanged.
steps: Both the restoring torque (mgL sin θ) and the rotational inertia (mL^2) are proportional to m.
m cancels, so T = 2π√(L/g) is unchanged.
items.skill: Explain why mass cancels

items.prompt: Compare sin θ with θ at 10° and at 30°, giving the percentage by which θ (in radians) exceeds sin θ in each case. What does this suggest about using T = 2π√(L/g) for a 30° swing?
items.answer: At 10°: θ = 0.1745 rad and sin θ = 0.1736, a difference of 0.51%. At 30°: θ = 0.5236 rad and sin θ = 0.5000, a difference of 4.7%. The small-angle formula is fine at 10° but noticeably inaccurate at 30° (the true period is a little longer).
steps: Convert to radians: 10° = 0.1745 rad and 30° = 0.5236 rad.
(θ − sin θ)/sin θ = 0.51% and 4.7%: the restoring torque is weaker than the linear approximation, so large swings take longer.
items.skill: Judge the small-angle approximation

worksheets.title: Physical pendulums
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A thin hoop of radius 0.20 m hangs on a peg at its top, as shown, and swings in its own plane. Find its period for small swings.
steps: Parallel axis: I = mR^2 + mR^2 = 2mR^2 about the peg, with d = R.
items.skill: Find the period of a hoop pendulum

items.prompt: A uniform rod of length L swings about a pivot a distance d from its center. Show that T = 2π√((L^2/12 + d^2)/(gd)). For L = 1.0 m, find the value of d that gives the shortest period, and that period.
steps: T is smallest where f(d) = L^2/(12d) + d is smallest: f′(d) = −L^2/(12d^2) + 1 = 0 gives d = L/√12 = 0.289 m, and T = 2π√(2(0.289)/9.8) = 1.53 s.
items.skill: Minimize a period with a derivative

items.prompt: A 1.8 kg irregular metal plate swings about a pivot 0.25 m from its center of mass with a period of 1.30 s. Find its rotational inertia about the pivot and about its center of mass.
items.answer: 0.19 kg·m^2 about the pivot; 0.076 kg·m^2 about the center of mass.
items.skill: Measure a rotational inertia from a period

items.prompt: A simple pendulum 0.50 m long hangs in an elevator. Find its period when the elevator is at rest and when it accelerates upward at 2.0 m/s^2, and explain the change.
items.answer: 1.42 s at rest; 1.29 s while accelerating upward. In the accelerating elevator the string must supply mg + ma, so the bob behaves as if g were 11.8 m/s^2, which shortens the period.
steps: In the elevator's frame the effective gravity is g + a = 11.8 m/s^2: T = 2π√(0.50/11.8) = 1.29 s.
items.skill: Use an effective g

items.prompt: A child sits on a swing, then stands up on the seat, raising her center of mass. How does the period of small swings change?
choices: It increases, because she is heavier when standing.
It decreases, because her center of mass is now closer to the pivot.
It is unchanged, because mass does not affect the period.
It increases, because her rotational inertia is larger.
items.answer: (B) It decreases, because her center of mass is now closer to the pivot.
steps: The swing behaves roughly like a pendulum whose length is the distance from the pivot to the center of mass.
Standing moves her center of mass up, shortening the effective length, so T decreases; her mass is the same either way.
items.skill: Reason about the effective length

items.prompt: A simple pendulum has a bob of mass m on a light string of length L. (a) Starting from the torque about the pivot, derive the equation of motion for θ. (b) State the approximation that makes the motion simple harmonic and when it is valid. (c) Show by substitution that θ(t) = θ_0 cos(√(g/L) t) satisfies the approximate equation. (d) For L = 0.60 m and θ_0 = 0.12 rad, find the period and the largest angular speed of the string.

rubric.criterion: (a) τ = −mgL sin θ and I = mL^2, so mL^2 d^2θ/dt^2 = −mgL sin θ, giving d^2θ/dt^2 = −(g/L) sin θ.
(b) sin θ ≈ θ (θ in radians), valid for small angles, roughly below 0.2 rad (about 10°).
(c) d^2θ/dt^2 = −θ_0(g/L) cos(√(g/L) t) = −(g/L)θ, so the equation holds.

items.answer: (a) d^2θ/dt^2 = −(g/L) sin θ. (b) sin θ ≈ θ for small angles in radians. (c) Substitution gives −(g/L)θ. (d) T = 1.55 s; 0.49 rad/s.
steps: The weight's lever arm about the pivot is L sin θ.
items.skill: Derive the pendulum equation

worksheets.title: Paper investigation: a rod pendulum
worksheets.directions:
Paper investigation. This is a paper investigation with supplied, invented data. It does not replace the hands-on laboratory work, at least 25% of instructional time, that College Board's framework for the AP® Physics C: Mechanics course calls for, and it does not count toward the AP Course Audit or college lab credit. A student hangs a uniform rod with a row of holes from a pin through one hole, as shown, and times 10 small oscillations (less than 10°) for six pivot positions. The distance d is measured from the pin to the rod's center.
| d (m) | 0.050 | 0.10 | 0.15 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.40 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| time for 10 oscillations (s) | 23.8 | 17.6 | 15.6 | 14.7 | 14.5 | 15.2 |

items.prompt: Find the period for each trial. Why did the student time 10 oscillations instead of one, and why keep the swings small?
items.answer: T = 2.38, 1.76, 1.56, 1.47, 1.45 and 1.52 s. Timing 10 oscillations divides the reaction-time error of starting and stopping the stopwatch by 10; small swings keep sin θ ≈ θ, so the period does not depend on amplitude and matches the model.
steps: T = (time for 10)/10.
A reaction-time error of about 0.2 s becomes 0.02 s per period; at large angles the period lengthens.
items.skill: Justify measurement choices

items.prompt: Use T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = m(L^2/12 + d^2) to show that T^2d = (4π^2/g)d^2 + (4π^2/g)(L^2/12). What should a graph of T^2d against d^2 look like?
items.answer: Squaring and multiplying by d gives T^2d = (4π^2/g)(d^2 + L^2/12): a straight line with slope 4π^2/g and vertical intercept 4π^2L^2/(12g).
steps: Multiply by d: T^2d = (4π^2/g)d^2 + 4π^2L^2/(12g), which has the form y = mx + b with x = d^2.
items.skill: Linearize a physical-pendulum model

items.prompt: Compute d^2 and T^2d for each trial, plot T^2d against d^2 on the grid provided, and draw a best-fit line.

rubric.criterion: Labels and scales both axes and plots the six points correctly.
Draws one straight best-fit line with a positive intercept.

items.answer: The six points, from (0.0025, 0.283) to (0.160, 0.924), lie close to a straight line.
steps: For example, the 0.20 m trial: T = 1.47 s, so T^2d = (1.47)^2(0.20) = 0.432 s^2·m.
The intercept is well above zero, so the axes should include the origin to show it.
items.skill: Plot linearized data

items.prompt: Find the slope and intercept of your best-fit line. Use the slope to find g and the intercept to find the length of the rod.
items.answer: Slope about 4.06 s^2/m (accept 3.9–4.2), so g = 4π^2/slope ≈ 9.7 m/s^2; intercept about 0.27 s^2·m (accept 0.25–0.29), so L^2/12 = intercept/slope = 0.067 m^2 and L ≈ 0.89 m.
steps: A least-squares fit gives slope 4.06 s^2/m and intercept 0.271 s^2·m.
items.skill: Extract physical quantities from a fit

items.prompt: From the table, the period is smallest near d = 0.25–0.30 m. Show that the model gives the shortest period at d = L/√12, and compare with your value of L.
items.answer: dT/dd = 0 where L^2/(12d^2) = 1, so d = L/√12; with L ≈ 0.89 m this is 0.26 m, between the 0.20 m and 0.30 m trials, consistent with the data (1.47 s and 1.45 s, both less than at 0.15 m and 0.40 m).
steps: T^2 ∝ L^2/(12d) + d, whose derivative −L^2/(12d^2) + 1 is zero at d = L/√12.
items.skill: Test a consequence of the model

items.prompt: Suppose the student had used swings of about 30°. Would the measured periods be too large or too small, and how would that affect the value of g found from the slope? Name one other source of error and its likely effect.
items.answer: Too large: at 30° the restoring torque is weaker than the small-angle model assumes, so each period is about 2% longer, the slope larger and g too small. Another source: friction at the pin, which damps the swing (little effect on the period but makes counting harder), or measuring d to the edge of the hole instead of the pin's center, which shifts every d^2 and changes the slope.
steps: The full equation has sin θ < θ, so the bob accelerates back more slowly and T increases.
g = 4π^2/slope, so a larger slope gives a smaller g.
items.skill: Analyze systematic error

items.prompt: Design a procedure to test whether the period of a simple pendulum depends on its amplitude, using a string, a bob, a protractor and a stopwatch (a version at home could use a washer on a thread; keep the swing clear of people and objects). Say what you would vary, what you would keep fixed, what you would measure and what graph you would make.
items.answer: Sample: keep the length (measured to the bob's center) and the bob fixed. Release from rest at amplitudes from 5° to 40° in steps of 5°, time 10 oscillations three times at each amplitude, and average. Plot T against amplitude: a flat line at small angles that rises at larger angles would show the limit of the small-angle model.
steps: Change only the amplitude; hold L and m constant.
Repeated timings of several oscillations reduce random error; the graph reveals any trend.
items.skill: Design an experiment on pendulum amplitude

weeks.title: Review: translational mechanics with calculus
weeks.objective: Consolidate Units 1–4 by theme, choosing among kinematics, Newton's second law, work–energy and impulse–momentum for forces given as functions of time, position or velocity, and translate fluently among equations, graphs, tables and words in the mathematical-routines and representation styles of the exam.

connection.before: Units 1–4: derivatives and integrals of motion (Weeks 1–5), Newton's laws with variable and resistive forces (Weeks 6–11), work, potential energy and power (Weeks 12–15), and impulse, momentum and collisions (Weeks 16–18).
connection.after: Week 32 reviews rotation, oscillations and experimental design; Week 33 is the timed practice exam.

days: Rates and accumulation: x, v and a by derivatives and integrals, in one and two dimensions, with graphs and tables.
Newton's second law with forces that depend on time, position or velocity; separating variables for linear drag.
Work, potential energy and power: ∫F dx, F = −dU/dx, energy accounting with friction, P = F·v.
Impulse, momentum and collisions: ∫F dt, conservation in one and two dimensions, center-of-mass motion.
Mixed practice: choosing the principle, translating between representations, and a short timed set.
explanation: Translational mechanics rests on four connected tools. Kinematics links position, velocity and acceleration by derivatives (v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt) and integrals (Δx = ∫v dt, Δv = ∫a dt). Newton's second law, ΣF = ma = dp/dt, links forces to acceleration. The work–energy theorem, W_net = ∫F dx = ΔK, and potential energy, F = −dU/dx, track energy over a displacement. The impulse–momentum theorem, J = ∫F dt = Δp, tracks momentum over a time interval. Each is a consequence of the second law, so they never disagree; they differ in which question they answer quickly.

Let the form of the force choose the tool. A force given as F(t) integrates directly over time, so use impulse and momentum for velocity, then integrate again for position. A force given as F(x) integrates directly over position, so use work and energy for speed, and F = −dU/dx with energy diagrams for equilibrium and turning points. A force that depends on velocity, such as linear drag −bv, goes into m dv/dt = F(v); now that separation of variables is available from calculus, write dv/(F(v)/m) = dt, integrate both sides, and apply the initial condition, or use a = v dv/dx when the question asks about distance. Interactions between objects call for momentum conservation when external impulses are negligible, and the center of mass moves as if all external forces acted on the total mass.

Graphs carry the same relations. The slope of x–t is v, the slope of v–t is a and its signed area is Δx; the area under F–t is the impulse and the slope of p–t is the net force; the area under F–x is the work, the slope of K–x is the net force, and the slope of U–x is −F. Mathematical-routines questions reward starting from one of these fundamental relations, keeping symbols until the end, and checking units and limiting cases. Representation questions reward sketches that agree with each other: where v crosses zero, x has a maximum or minimum; where F changes sign, the slope of v changes sign.

Common errors in review: integrating a force over time and calling the result work, or over distance and calling it impulse; dropping the constant of integration (an initial velocity or position); adding kinetic energies when momentum is what is conserved in a collision; forgetting the vertical component of a pull when finding a normal force; and assuming static friction equals μ_sN instead of whatever the equilibrium needs, up to that limit. Before calculating, write which principle you are using and why it fits the given information.

figures.alt: Graph of net force F in newtons against time t in seconds from 0 to 6 s. F rises in a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 6.0 N at t = 2.0 s, stays at 6.0 N until t = 4.0 s, then drops to −2.0 N and stays there until t = 6.0 s.
figures.caption: Net force on the 2.0 kg cart

figures.alt: Blank axes for a sketch: velocity v in m/s from −4 to 8 on the vertical axis and time t in seconds from 0 to 6 on the horizontal axis, with grid lines.

Key graph of v against t: a curve that starts at −3.0 m/s at t = 0, rises with increasing slope to 0 at t = 2.0 s, then a straight line rising to 6.0 m/s at t = 4.0 s, then a straight line falling to 4.0 m/s at t = 6.0 s.
figures.caption: Velocity of the cart

figures.alt: Graph of potential energy U in joules against position x in meters from 0 to 6 m. U falls in a straight line from 4.0 J at x = 0 to −2.0 J at x = 2.0 m, is flat at −2.0 J from x = 2.0 m to x = 4.0 m, then rises in a straight line to 6.0 J at x = 6.0 m. A dashed horizontal line marks 2.0 J.
figures.caption: Potential energy of the particle

figures.alt: Key graph of force F in newtons against x in meters: F = +3.0 N from x = 0 to 2.0 m, 0 from 2.0 m to 4.0 m, and −4.0 N from 4.0 m to 6.0 m.
figures.caption: Force on the particle

figures.alt: Position–time graph from t = 0 to 4.0 s. Line A rises from x = 0 at t = 0 to x = 3.0 m at t = 2.0 s. Line B falls from x = 6.0 m at t = 0 to x = 3.0 m at t = 2.0 s. From t = 2.0 s to 4.0 s a single line rises from x = 3.0 m to x = 4.0 m.
figures.caption: Positions of carts A and B

figures.alt: Key: the same position–time graph with a dashed straight line for the center of mass, rising from x = 2.0 m at t = 0 through x = 3.0 m at t = 2.0 s to x = 4.0 m at t = 4.0 s.
figures.caption: Center of mass of the two carts

examples.prompt: A 1.5 kg drone rises vertically from rest. Its rotors push up with a thrust T(t) = 18 + 3.0t, in newtons with t in seconds, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.0 s. Take up as positive. Find the net impulse on the drone, its velocity and height at t = 4.0 s, and the work done by the thrust.
examples.answer: Net impulse 37 N·s (37.2 N·s) upward; v = 24.8 m/s upward; height 38.9 m; work by the thrust 1.03 × 10^3 J (1034 J).
steps: The force is given as a function of time, so start with impulse. The net force is F(t) = 18 + 3.0t − (1.5)(9.8) = 3.3 + 3.0t newtons.
The thrust's work is ∫T v dt = ∫ from 0 to 4.0 of (18 + 3.0t)(2.2t + t^2) dt = [19.8t^2 + 8.2t^3 + 0.75t^4] from 0 to 4.0 = 1034 J.
Check with energy: ΔK + ΔU = ½(1.5)(24.8)^2 + (1.5)(9.8)(38.9) = 461 + 572 = 1034 J, which matches.

examples.prompt: A 0.50 kg block is pushed against a spring (k = 400 N/m) at the bottom of a 30° incline, compressing it 0.12 m, and released from rest. The spring is fixed at the bottom and is not attached to the block. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20 and the coefficient of static friction is 0.35. How far up the incline, from its release point, does the block travel? Does it stay at its highest point?
examples.answer: It travels 0.87 m (0.873 m) up the incline from its release point, then slides back down, because the static friction needed, 2.45 N, exceeds the 1.49 N available.
steps: Only positions matter (start, top), so use energy: the spring's stored energy goes into gravitational potential energy and work against friction. The block leaves the spring at its natural length but keeps moving.
½kx^2 = ½(400)(0.12)^2 = 2.88 J. Over a distance d along the incline, the block rises d sin 30° and friction does −μ_k mg cos 30° d.
2.88 = mg d(sin 30° + μ_k cos 30°) = (0.50)(9.8)d(0.500 + 0.173) = 3.30d, so d = 0.873 m (d is larger than 0.12 m, so the block does leave the spring).
At the top, gravity's component along the incline is mg sin 30° = 2.45 N, but static friction can supply at most μ_s mg cos 30° = (0.35)(0.50)(9.8)(0.866) = 1.49 N, so the block slides back.

examples.prompt: A 1500 kg rail car coasts at 8.0 m/s on a level track. Air and rolling resistance together act like a linear drag force of size bv, with b = 60 kg/s, and no other horizontal forces act. Use separation of variables to find v(t). How long does the car take to slow to 2.0 m/s, how far does it travel meanwhile, and how far would it travel before stopping?
examples.answer: v(t) = (8.0 m/s)e^(−t/25 s); 35 s (34.7 s) to slow to 2.0 m/s, covering 150 m; total distance 200 m.
steps: Newton's second law with the direction of motion positive: m dv/dt = −bv, so dv/v = −(b/m) dt.
Integrate from v_0 at t = 0 to v at t: ln(v/v_0) = −(b/m)t, so v = v_0 e^(−bt/m) with m/b = 1500/60 = 25 s.
For distance use a = v dv/dx: mv dv/dx = −bv gives dv/dx = −b/m, so v = v_0 − (b/m)x. From 8.0 to 2.0 m/s: x = (6.0 m/s)(25 s) = 150 m.
Setting v = 0 gives x = v_0 m/b = (8.0)(25) = 200 m, reached only as t grows without bound.

worksheets.title: Kinematics and dynamics by calculus
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A car moving at 4.0 m/s at t = 0 has acceleration a(t) = 3.0 − 0.50t, in m/s^2 with t in seconds, along its direction of motion. When is its speed greatest, and what is that speed?
items.answer: (A) At t = 6.0 s; 13 m/s
steps: v(t) = 4.0 + 3.0t − 0.25t^2; the speed is greatest where a = dv/dt = 0, at t = 6.0 s.
v(6.0) = 4.0 + 18 − 9.0 = 13 m/s. (22 m/s omits the −0.25t^2 term; 12 s is when v returns to 4.0 m/s.)
items.skill: Find an extreme speed from a(t)

items.prompt: A particle moving in a plane has velocity v(t) = (4.0 − 2.0t) i + 3.0 j, in m/s with t in seconds, and is at the origin at t = 0. (a) When is its speed least, and what is it? (b) Where is the particle then? (c) Find the angle between its velocity and acceleration at t = 1.0 s, and say whether it is speeding up or slowing down then.
items.answer: (a) At t = 2.0 s, 3.0 m/s. (b) At (4.0 m, 6.0 m). (c) 124° (123.7°); greater than 90°, so it is slowing down.
steps: (a) Speed^2 = (4.0 − 2.0t)^2 + 9.0 is least when 4.0 − 2.0t = 0, at t = 2.0 s, where the speed is 3.0 m/s.
A component of a opposite to v reduces the speed.
items.skill: Use vector derivatives and the dot product

items.prompt: A 3.0 kg block sits on a ramp inclined at 35°. A light string tied to it runs up the ramp, over a light frictionless pulley at the top, and down to a hanging 2.5 kg block. Between the block and the ramp, μ_s = 0.30 and μ_k = 0.25. The blocks are released from rest. (a) Show that the blocks start to move, and state which way. (b) Find their acceleration. (c) Find the tension in the string.

rubric.criterion: Compares the unbalanced pull, m_2g − m_1g sin 35° = 24.5 − 16.9 = 7.6 N, with the largest static friction, μ_s m_1g cos 35° = 7.2 N, and concludes that the blocks move, with the hanging block going down.
Uses kinetic friction, μ_k m_1g cos 35° = 6.0 N, directed down the ramp, opposite the motion.
Finds T = m_2(g − a) = 23.8 N (accept 23.7–23.9 N), and checks it with the ramp block's equation.

items.answer: (a) The blocks move, with the hanging block descending: 7.6 N of unbalanced pull exceeds the 7.2 N of static friction available. (b) a = 0.29 m/s^2. (c) T = 23.8 N.
steps: Take the direction in which the hanging block descends as positive for both blocks.
Gravity along the ramp on the 3.0 kg block: (3.0)(9.8) sin 35° = 16.9 N; hanging weight 24.5 N; normal force (3.0)(9.8) cos 35° = 24.1 N.
Static check: 24.5 − 16.9 = 7.6 N > μ_s N = 7.2 N, so they slip; kinetic friction is 0.25(24.1) = 6.0 N.
items.skill: Apply the second law to a connected system with friction

items.prompt: A car starts from rest on a circular track of radius 40 m and speeds up with a constant tangential acceleration of 1.5 m/s^2. At what time is its centripetal acceleration equal in size to its tangential acceleration?
items.skill: Combine tangential and centripetal acceleration

items.prompt: A 0.10 kg ball is released from rest in a tall column of glycerin, which exerts a drag force of size bv with b = 0.050 kg/s. Ignore buoyancy and take down as positive. (a) Write Newton's second law and separate variables to derive v(t). (b) Find the terminal speed and the time constant. (c) How long after release does the ball reach 90% of its terminal speed?

rubric.criterion: Writes m dv/dt = mg − bv and separates it as dv/(mg/b − v) = (b/m) dt.
Integrates with v(0) = 0 to get v(t) = v_T(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with v_T = mg/b and τ = m/b.
Finds v_T = 19.6 m/s, τ = 2.0 s and t = τ ln 10 = 4.6 s.

steps: Separate: dv/(v_T − v) = dt/τ. Integrating from 0 to v gives −ln[(v_T − v)/v_T] = t/τ.
items.skill: Solve a drag equation by separating variables

items.prompt: A 1.5 kg package hangs from a spring scale attached to the ceiling of an elevator. The elevator's height is y(t) = 2.0t^2 − 0.20t^3, in meters with t in seconds and up positive. What does the scale read at t = 1.0 s?
steps: The scale's force F satisfies F − mg = ma, so F = 1.5(9.8 + 2.8) = 18.9 N.
items.skill: Find a force from a position function

worksheets.title: Energy and momentum
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A horizontal force F(x) = 6.0√(x), in newtons with x in meters, pushes a 2.0 kg cart along a level frictionless track. The cart starts from rest at x = 0. What is its speed at x = 4.0 m?
items.skill: Integrate a position-dependent force

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg steel ball hangs on a light string 1.0 m long. It is pulled out until the string is horizontal and released from rest. At the bottom of its swing it collides elastically with a 1.5 kg block at rest on a level floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is 0.30. (a) Find the ball's speed just before the collision. (b) Find the velocities of the ball and the block just after the collision. (c) How far does the block slide? (d) How high does the ball rise after the collision?

rubric.criterion: Uses energy conservation for the swing: v = √(2gL) = 4.4 m/s (4.43 m/s).
Uses momentum conservation and the elastic condition (or the standard results) to get the block at 2.2 m/s forward and the ball at 2.2 m/s backward.
Uses work–energy for the block: d = v^2/(2μ_k g) = 0.83 m (accept 0.82–0.84 m).
Finds the ball's rebound height h = v^2/(2g) = 0.25 m.

items.answer: (a) 4.4 m/s. (b) Ball 2.2 m/s backward; block 2.2 m/s forward. (c) 0.83 m. (d) 0.25 m.
items.skill: Chain energy, momentum and work–energy stages

items.prompt: Carts P and Q move at the same speed on a level track. Cart Q has twice the mass of cart P. Each is stopped by the same constant braking force. How do Q's stopping time and stopping distance compare with P's?
choices: Q's time is twice P's; Q's distance is twice P's.
Q's time is twice P's; Q's distance is four times P's.
Q's time equals P's; Q's distance is twice P's.
Q's time is √(2) times P's; Q's distance is twice P's.
items.answer: (A) Q's time is twice P's; Q's distance is twice P's.
steps: Impulse: FΔt = Δp = mv, so the stopping time is proportional to the momentum, which is twice as large for Q.
Work: Fd = ½mv^2, so the stopping distance is proportional to the kinetic energy, which is also twice as large for Q.
items.skill: Contrast impulse and work for stopping

items.prompt: A 0.30 kg puck moving at 4.0 m/s along +x on a level air table strikes a 0.20 kg puck at rest. Afterward the 0.30 kg puck moves at 30° above the +x-axis and the 0.20 kg puck moves at 45° below the +x-axis. (a) Find the speed of each puck after the collision. (b) Is the collision elastic? Support your answer with a calculation.

rubric.criterion: Writes momentum conservation in both directions: 1.2 = 0.30v_1 cos 30° + 0.20v_2 cos 45° and 0 = 0.30v_1 sin 30° − 0.20v_2 sin 45°.
Solves to get v_2 = 1.06v_1.
Finds v_1 = 2.9 m/s (2.93) and v_2 = 3.1 m/s (3.11), accepting ±1 in the last digit.
Compares kinetic energies, 2.40 J before and 2.25 J after, and concludes that the collision is not elastic (about 6% is lost).

items.answer: (a) The 0.30 kg puck moves at 2.9 m/s and the 0.20 kg puck at 3.1 m/s. (b) No: kinetic energy drops from 2.40 J to 2.25 J.
items.skill: Solve a two-dimensional collision

items.prompt: A small meteoroid starts from rest relative to Earth at a distance of 2R_E from Earth's center, where R_E is Earth's radius, and falls straight in. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving when it reaches the surface? Use G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2, Earth's mass 5.97 × 10^24 kg and R_E = 6.37 × 10^6 m.
steps: Energy: −GMm/(2R_E) = ½mv^2 − GMm/R_E, so v^2 = GM/R_E.
items.skill: Use the 1/r gravitational potential energy

items.prompt: A 900 kg car's engine delivers a constant 36 kW to its wheels. Ignore friction and drag. The car is moving at 10 m/s on a level road. (a) How long does it take to reach 20 m/s? (b) Use F = P/v and a = v dv/dx to find the distance it covers meanwhile.

rubric.criterion: Uses P = dK/dt with constant P: t = ΔK/P = ½(900)(20^2 − 10^2)/36000 = 3.75 s.
Writes mv dv/dx = P/v, so mv^2 dv = P dx.
Integrates to get x = m(v_2^3 − v_1^3)/(3P) = 58 m.

items.skill: Integrate with constant power

worksheets.title: Translating between representations
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: The graph shows the net force on a 2.0 kg cart that moves along a level track. At t = 0 the cart's velocity is −3.0 m/s. (a) At what time is the cart momentarily at rest? (b) On the axes provided, sketch the cart's velocity from t = 0 to t = 6.0 s, labeling the values at t = 2.0 s, 4.0 s and 6.0 s. (c) When is the cart's speed greatest? (d) Find the net work done on the cart from t = 0 to t = 6.0 s.

rubric.criterion: Uses the area under F–t: the impulse from 0 to 2.0 s is 6.0 N·s, which brings the velocity from −3.0 m/s to 0 at t = 2.0 s.
Finds v = 6.0 m/s at t = 4.0 s (12 N·s more) and 4.0 m/s at t = 6.0 s (−4.0 N·s).
Sketch: concave-up curve from −3.0 to 0 on 0–2 s (slope growing with F), straight rise to 6.0 on 2–4 s, straight fall to 4.0 on 4–6 s.
States the greatest speed is 6.0 m/s at t = 4.0 s, where F changes sign.

items.answer: (a) t = 2.0 s. (b) See the key graph: −3.0 m/s rising to 0 at 2.0 s, 6.0 m/s at 4.0 s, 4.0 m/s at 6.0 s. (c) At t = 4.0 s, 6.0 m/s. (d) 7.0 J.
steps: On 0–2 s the force grows linearly, so v rises along a parabola that gets steeper; the slope of v–t equals F/m throughout.
items.skill: Translate a force graph into velocity

items.prompt: The momentum of a cart moving along a line is p(t) = 4.0t − t^2, in kg·m/s with t in seconds. Which statement describes the net force on the cart?
choices: It decreases linearly and is zero at t = 2.0 s.
It is zero at t = 4.0 s, when the cart stops.
items.answer: (B) It decreases linearly and is zero at t = 2.0 s.
steps: The net force is dp/dt = 4.0 − 2.0t newtons.
That decreases linearly and is zero at t = 2.0 s, where the momentum is greatest; at t = 4.0 s the momentum is zero but the force is −4.0 N.
items.skill: Read force as the slope of momentum

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg particle moves along the x-axis with the potential energy shown. Its total mechanical energy is 2.0 J (dashed line). (a) Find its turning points. (b) Sketch the force on the particle as a function of x from x = 0 to x = 6.0 m. (c) Find the particle's speed between x = 2.0 m and x = 4.0 m. (d) Describe its motion.

rubric.criterion: Finds the turning points where U = E: x = 0.67 m (from 4.0 − 3.0x = 2.0) and x = 5.0 m (from −2.0 + 4.0(x − 4.0) = 2.0).
Uses F = −dU/dx to get F = +3.0 N on 0–2 m, 0 on 2–4 m and −4.0 N on 4–6 m, and sketches these constant pieces.
Describes back-and-forth motion between 0.67 m and 5.0 m: speeding up on the left slope, constant speed in the flat region, slowing on the right slope.

items.answer: (a) x = 0.67 m and x = 5.0 m. (b) F = +3.0 N, then 0, then −4.0 N (key graph). (c) 4.0 m/s. (d) It moves back and forth between the turning points.
steps: Left piece: U = 4.0 − 3.0x; right piece: U = −2.0 + 4.0(x − 4.0).
Turning points: 4.0 − 3.0x = 2.0 gives x = 0.667 m; −2.0 + 4.0(x − 4.0) = 2.0 gives x = 5.0 m.
Flat region: ½(0.50)v^2 = 4.0 J, v = 4.0 m/s.
items.skill: Translate a potential-energy graph

items.prompt: A student solves a problem with the equation ½(2.0)v^2 = (2.0)(9.8)(1.5) − (0.30)(2.0)(9.8)(cos 30°)(3.0). Which situation does it describe?
choices: A 2.0 kg block is released from rest and slides 1.5 m down a 30° incline with μ_k = 0.30.
A 2.0 kg block slides 3.0 m across a level floor with μ_k = 0.30 after falling 1.5 m.
A 2.0 kg block is released from rest and slides 3.0 m down a 30° incline with μ_k = 0.30.
A 2.0 kg block is pushed 3.0 m up a 30° incline with μ_k = 0.30 and rises 1.5 m.
items.answer: (C) A 2.0 kg block is released from rest and slides 3.0 m down a 30° incline with μ_k = 0.30.
steps: The first term on the right is the drop in gravitational energy, mgh with h = 1.5 m; 3.0 m along a 30° incline drops exactly 3.0 sin 30° = 1.5 m.
The second term is friction's work over 3.0 m with normal force mg cos 30°, and the left side is the final kinetic energy from rest, so the block slides down.
items.skill: Match an energy equation to a situation

items.prompt: The graph shows the positions of carts A and B, which move along a level track, collide at t = 2.0 s and stick together. Cart A's mass is 2.0 kg. (a) Find each cart's velocity before the collision and their common velocity after. (b) Find cart B's mass. (c) Find the kinetic energy lost in the collision. (d) Sketch the position of the two-cart system's center of mass from t = 0 to 4.0 s.

rubric.criterion: Reads the slopes: A at +1.5 m/s, B at −1.5 m/s, and the joined carts at +0.50 m/s.
Uses momentum conservation, 2.0(1.5) + m_B(−1.5) = (2.0 + m_B)(0.50), to find m_B = 1.0 kg.
Finds kinetic energy 3.375 J before and 0.375 J after, so 3.0 J is lost.
Sketches a straight line for x_cm from 2.0 m at t = 0 to 4.0 m at t = 4.0 s (slope 0.50 m/s), continuous through the collision.

items.answer: (a) A: +1.5 m/s; B: −1.5 m/s; after: +0.50 m/s. (b) 1.0 kg. (c) 3.0 J. (d) A straight line from 2.0 m to 4.0 m (key graph).
steps: x_cm(0) = (2.0 × 0 + 1.0 × 6.0)/3.0 = 2.0 m, and v_cm = total momentum/total mass = 1.5/3.0 = 0.50 m/s throughout.
items.skill: Translate a position graph into momentum and energy

items.prompt:
A motion sensor records a 2.0 kg cart's position on a level track. Which statement about the net force on the cart is supported by the data?
| t (s) | 0 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| x (m) | 0 | 0.50 | 2.00 | 4.50 | 8.00 |
choices: It is zero, because the cart moves the same distance each second.
It increases steadily, because the distance covered each second increases.
items.answer: (D) It is 2.0 N and constant.
steps: The distances covered each second are 0.50, 1.50, 2.50 and 3.50 m; their differences are constant, 1.00 m, so a = 1.00 m/s^2 (x = 0.50t^2).
F = ma = (2.0)(1.0) = 2.0 N, constant.
items.skill: Infer a force from position data

weeks.title: Review: rotation, oscillation, and experimental design
weeks.objective: Consolidate Units 5–7, using the rotational second law, rotational energy, angular momentum, orbital conservation laws and the conditions for simple harmonic motion, and plan, linearize and analyze an investigation with supplied data in the experimental-design style of the exam.

connection.before: Week 31's review of Units 1–4; Units 5–7: torque, rotational inertia and Στ = Iα (Weeks 19–23), rotational energy, angular momentum, rolling and orbits (Weeks 24–27), and oscillations and pendulums (Weeks 28–30).
connection.after: Week 33 is the timed practice exam, then self-scoring and error analysis.

days: Rotational dynamics: Στ = Iα for wheels, rods and connected systems, with torques that change in time.
Rotational energy and angular momentum: rolling, collisions with a pivot, changing rotational inertia, and orbits.
Oscillations: identifying SHM from a force or torque, ω^2 = k/m and mgd/I, energy and initial conditions.
Experimental design: variables, linearization, slope and intercept meanings, uncertainty and systematic error, with a torsion-pendulum data set.
Mixed practice and a short timed set in the qualitative/quantitative style.
explanation: Rotation repeats the translational toolkit with new symbols: θ, ω = dθ/dt and α = dω/dt for x, v and a; torque τ = r × F for force; rotational inertia I = ∫r^2 dm for mass; Στ = Iα for ΣF = ma; K = ½Iω^2 and W = ∫τ dθ for kinetic energy and work; L = Iω, and L = r × p for a particle, with Στ = dL/dt for momentum. Rolling without slipping ties the two descriptions together with v_cm = Rω and a_cm = Rα, and its kinetic energy splits into ½Mv_cm^2 + ½I_cmω^2.

Choose the rotational principle the same way as the translational one. A torque given in time integrates to angular impulse, ∫τ dt = ΔL. A torque given in angle integrates to work, ∫τ dθ = ΔK. Collisions with a fixed pivot, or a body whose rotational inertia changes while no external torque acts, conserve angular momentum about that pivot even though the pivot's force means linear momentum is not conserved. For orbits, gravity exerts no torque about the planet's center, so L is conserved, and gravity is conservative, so E = ½mv^2 − GMm/r is conserved; together they give speeds at the nearest and farthest points of an ellipse.

A system moves in simple harmonic motion when its restoring force or torque is proportional to its displacement: F = −kx gives ω = √(k/m), and τ = −κθ gives ω = √(κ/I). For a physical pendulum, κ = mgd for small angles, so T = 2π√(I/(mgd)). Find κ for an unfamiliar system by writing the torque for a small angle and keeping the term proportional to θ. Energy fixes amplitude, A = √(x_0^2 + (v_0/ω)^2), and the period never depends on the amplitude in SHM.

Experimental-design questions ask for a procedure, a straight-line graph, and the meaning of its slope and intercept. Identify the independent variable you change, the dependent variable you measure, and what you hold constant. Rearrange the model so that it reads y = (slope)x + (intercept) with measured quantities on the axes, and draw a best-fit line rather than using two data points. Repeated timing of many oscillations reduces the relative uncertainty of a period. A constant offset in a measurement usually shifts the intercept; a proportional error changes the slope. This is a paper investigation with supplied, invented data. It does not replace the hands-on laboratory work, at least 25% of instructional time, that College Board's framework for the AP® Physics C: Mechanics course calls for, and it does not count toward the AP Course Audit or college lab credit.

Common errors in review: using the distance to the force's point of application instead of the lever arm; taking I about the center of mass for a body that pivots at its end; conserving kinetic energy in a collision with a pivot; forgetting that a rolling body's static friction does no work but does change its spin; using the length of a physical pendulum instead of the distance d from the pivot to the center of mass; and fitting a line through the origin when the model has an intercept.

figures.caption: T^2 against r^2

examples.prompt: A turntable with rotational inertia 0.20 kg·m^2 starts from rest. A motor applies a torque τ(t) = 0.80 − 0.20t, in N·m with t in seconds, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.0 s, then stops. Next, a 0.40 kg block, at first resting at the axis, slides outward along a frictionless radial groove until it stops against the rim, 0.30 m from the axis. Find the angular velocity at t = 4.0 s and after the block reaches the rim. What happens to the rotational kinetic energy?
examples.answer: ω = 8.0 rad/s at 4.0 s; 6.8 rad/s after the block reaches the rim. Rotational kinetic energy falls from 6.4 J to 5.4 J; about 1.0 J is the block's outward motion, dissipated when it hits the rim.
steps: The torque is given in time, so use angular impulse: ΔL = ∫ from 0 to 4.0 of (0.80 − 0.20t) dt = 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6 kg·m^2/s, so ω = 1.6/0.20 = 8.0 rad/s.
No external torque acts about the axis while the block slides, so L is conserved: I' = 0.20 + (0.40)(0.30)^2 = 0.236 kg·m^2 and ω' = 1.6/0.236 = 6.78 rad/s.
Rotational kinetic energy: ½(0.20)(8.0)^2 = 6.4 J before; ½(0.236)(6.78)^2 = 5.42 J after.
The groove pushes the block around but not outward, so the block also gains outward speed; that 0.98 J of radial kinetic energy is lost in the stop at the rim.

examples.prompt: A uniform 0.40 kg rod 0.60 m long lies on a frictionless horizontal table and turns about a vertical axle through its center. A horizontal spring (k = 30 N/m) is attached to one end, perpendicular to the rod, and is relaxed when the rod is in the position shown. Show that small rotations are simple harmonic, and find the angular frequency and period.
examples.answer: τ ≈ −k(L/2)^2 θ, so ω = √(3k/m) = 15 rad/s and T = 0.42 s.
steps: Rotate the rod through a small angle θ. The spring's end moves about (L/2)θ, so the spring pulls back with about k(L/2)θ, perpendicular to the rod.
Its torque about the axle is τ ≈ −(L/2)·k(L/2)θ = −k(L/2)^2 θ: a restoring torque proportional to θ, so the motion is SHM with κ = k(L/2)^2 = (30)(0.30)^2 = 2.7 N·m/rad.
T = 2π/ω = 0.42 s. In symbols ω^2 = 3k/m, independent of L.

examples.prompt:
A student rolls a ball up a straight ramp tilted 10° above the horizontal and measures its speed v at the bottom and the distance d it rolls up the ramp before stopping. Rolling without slipping, d = (1 + β)v^2/(2g sin θ), where I = βMR^2. What should be graphed to give a straight line, and what does the data show about β?
| v (m/s) | 0.50 | 0.80 | 1.10 | 1.40 | 1.70 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| d (m) | 0.104 | 0.262 | 0.500 | 0.803 | 1.192 |
examples.answer: Graph d against v^2; the slope is about 0.411 s^2/m, so β = 0.40, as for a uniform solid ball.
steps: The model says d is proportional to v^2, so plot d (vertical) against v^2 (horizontal): v^2 = 0.25, 0.64, 1.21, 1.96 and 2.89 m^2/s^2.
A best-fit line through the points has slope about 0.411 s^2/m and passes near the origin, as the model requires.
β = 0.40, matching a uniform solid sphere (I = (2/5)MR^2).

worksheets.title: Rotation: dynamics, energy and angular momentum
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A grinding wheel with rotational inertia 0.30 kg·m^2 slows according to ω(t) = 40 − 2.0t^2, in rad/s with t in seconds. What net torque acts on it at t = 2.0 s?
steps: τ = Iα = (0.30)(−8.0) = −2.4 N·m, opposite the rotation.
items.skill: Find a torque from ω(t)

items.prompt: A 1.0 kg block on a smooth ramp inclined at 30° is tied to a string that runs parallel to the ramp, over a pulley at the top, to a hanging 2.0 kg block, as shown. The pulley is a uniform 2.0 kg disk of radius 0.10 m on a frictionless axle, and the string does not slip. Find the acceleration of the blocks and the tension in each part of the string.

rubric.criterion: Writes the second law for each block: (2.0)(9.8) − T_2 = 2.0a and T_1 − (1.0)(9.8) sin 30° = 1.0a.
Writes Στ = Iα for the pulley with α = a/R: (T_2 − T_1)R = ½MR^2(a/R).
Solves for a = 3.7 m/s^2 (3.68), with the hanging block moving down.
Finds T_2 = 12.3 N (12.25) on the hanging side and T_1 = 8.6 N (8.58) on the ramp side.

items.answer: a = 3.7 m/s^2 (3.68 m/s^2), hanging block down; tension 12.3 N on the hanging side and 8.6 N on the ramp side.
steps: Adding the three equations eliminates the tensions: a = (m_2g − m_1g sin 30°)/(m_1 + m_2 + M/2) = (19.6 − 4.9)/4.0 = 3.675 m/s^2.
items.skill: Combine translational and rotational second laws

items.prompt: A uniform rod 1.0 m long turns freely about a horizontal axle through one end. It is released from rest pointing 30° above the horizontal. What is its angular speed when it hangs straight down?
items.answer: (D) 6.6 rad/s
steps: The center of mass falls from 0.25 m above the axle to 0.50 m below it, a drop of 0.75 m.
Mg(0.75 m) = ½(ML^2/3)ω^2 gives ω^2 = 6g(0.75)/L^2 = 44.1 rad^2/s^2, so ω = 6.6 rad/s. (5.4 rad/s is the result for a horizontal release.)
items.skill: Use energy for a pivoted rod

items.prompt: A uniform 1.5 kg disk of radius 0.20 m lies flat and is free to turn about a fixed vertical axle through its center. It is at rest. A 0.050 kg dart moving horizontally at 12 m/s hits the disk's rim and sticks there; the dart's path passes 0.12 m from the axle. (a) Explain why angular momentum about the axle is conserved but linear momentum is not. (b) Find the disk's angular speed after the impact. (c) How much kinetic energy is lost?

rubric.criterion: Explains that the axle's force acts at the axis, so it exerts no torque about the axle, while it does supply an external impulse that changes linear momentum.
Uses L = mvr_⊥ = (0.050)(12)(0.12) = 0.072 kg·m^2/s for the dart about the axle.
Uses I = ½MR^2 + mR^2 = 0.032 kg·m^2 (the dart ends at the rim) and finds ω = 2.25 rad/s.
Finds kinetic energy 3.6 J before and 0.081 J after, so 3.5 J is lost.

items.answer: (a) The axle's force has no lever arm about the axle. (b) ω = 2.25 rad/s (2.3 rad/s). (c) 3.5 J.
steps: Before: L = mvr_⊥ with r_⊥ = 0.12 m, the perpendicular distance from the axle to the dart's line of motion.
items.skill: Conserve angular momentum about a pivot

items.prompt: A drill's motor delivers 450 W to the bit while it turns at a steady 2800 revolutions per minute. What torque does the motor exert on the bit?
steps: Convert: ω = 2800 × 2π/60 = 293 rad/s.
P = τω gives τ = 450/293 = 1.5 N·m. (0.16 N·m divides by revolutions per minute without converting.)
items.skill: Relate power, torque and angular speed

items.prompt: Two identical uniform rods, each of mass M and length L, rest on frictionless ice. Each receives the same brief horizontal impulse J perpendicular to its length: rod 1 at its center and rod 2 at one end. (a) Without calculating, state which rod has more kinetic energy afterward, and explain. (b) Derive each rod's center-of-mass speed and angular speed. (c) Find the ratio of their kinetic energies.

rubric.criterion: Claims rod 2 has more kinetic energy because it gets the same translational motion and also spins.
Uses J = Mv_cm for both rods, so v_cm = J/M for each.
Uses the angular impulse about the center for rod 2, J(L/2) = (ML^2/12)ω, so ω = 6J/(ML), and ω = 0 for rod 1.

items.answer: (a) Rod 2. (b) Both have v_cm = J/M; rod 1 does not spin and rod 2 spins at ω = 6J/(ML). (c) K_2/K_1 = 4.
steps: The impulse changes the total momentum by J whatever the point of application, so v_cm = J/M for both.
Rod 2: angular impulse about the center of mass equals the change in L_cm: J(L/2) = (ML^2/12)ω.
items.skill: Compare translation and rotation from an impulse

worksheets.title: Oscillations, pendulums and orbits
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2, Earth's mass 5.97 × 10^24 kg and Earth's radius 6.37 × 10^6 m where needed.

items.prompt: An oscillator's position is x(t) = 0.050 sin(8.0t + 0.50), in meters with t in seconds and the angle in radians. What is its velocity at t = 0?
steps: v(0) = 0.40 cos(0.50) = 0.35 m/s. (0.40 m/s is the greatest speed, not the value at t = 0.)
items.skill: Differentiate a sinusoidal position

items.prompt: A 1.0 kg block on a frictionless level surface is attached to a horizontal spring (k = 60 N/m), and a 0.50 kg block rests on top of it, as shown. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is 0.40. (a) Find the period of oscillation when the blocks move together. (b) Find the largest amplitude for which the top block does not slip. (c) At that amplitude, what is the greatest friction force on the top block, and where does it occur?

rubric.criterion: Uses the total mass on the spring: T = 2π√((1.0 + 0.50)/60) = 0.99 s.
States that static friction alone accelerates the top block, so its greatest acceleration, ω^2A, must not exceed μ_s g.
Finds the greatest friction force, m_top μ_s g = 1.96 N (2.0 N), at the turning points, x = ±A.

items.answer: (a) 0.99 s. (b) 0.098 m (9.8 cm). (c) 2.0 N (1.96 N), at the ends of the motion.
steps: The top block's acceleration is −ω^2x; it is largest at x = ±A.
items.skill: Combine SHM with static friction

items.prompt: A block on a spring moves as x(t) = A cos(ωt) with period T. What is the ratio of its kinetic energy to its spring potential energy at t = T/8?
steps: At t = T/8, ωt = π/4, so x = A cos(π/4) = A/√(2) and U = ½k(A^2/2) = ½ of the total energy.
The rest of the energy is kinetic, so K = U and the ratio is 1.
items.skill: Split oscillator energy at a given time

items.prompt: A satellite moves on an elliptical orbit around Earth. Its nearest distance from Earth's center is 6.8 × 10^6 m and its farthest is 2.04 × 10^7 m. (a) Explain why the satellite's angular momentum about Earth's center is constant. (b) Use conservation of angular momentum and of energy to find its speeds at the nearest and farthest points. (c) Compare the nearest-point speed with the speed of a circular orbit of radius 6.8 × 10^6 m.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Earth's gravity points toward Earth's center, so it exerts no torque about that point.
Writes r_1v_1 = r_2v_2 (speed perpendicular to r at both ends) and ½v_1^2 − GM/r_1 = ½v_2^2 − GM/r_2.
Finds the circular speed √(GM/r_1) = 7.65 × 10^3 m/s and notes the satellite at its nearest point moves faster than that, which is why it climbs away from Earth.

items.answer: (a) Gravity is a central force. (b) 9.37 × 10^3 m/s nearest; 3.12 × 10^3 m/s farthest. (c) Circular speed 7.65 × 10^3 m/s; the satellite is faster.
items.skill: Use angular momentum and energy for an orbit

items.prompt: A block on a spring oscillates on a level frictionless surface with period T. The same spring and block are set up on a frictionless incline at 30°, with the spring along the incline. What is the period now?
items.answer: (A) T
steps: On the incline, gravity's component along the slope only shifts the equilibrium position, by mg sin 30°/k.
Measured from the new equilibrium, the net force is still −kx, so ω = √(k/m) and the period is unchanged.
items.skill: Identify what sets an oscillator's period

items.prompt: A uniform 0.30 kg rod 0.50 m long hangs from a pivot at its top end, and a small 0.20 kg ball is fixed to its bottom end. (a) Find the system's rotational inertia about the pivot and the distance from the pivot to its center of mass. (b) Find the period of small oscillations. (c) Compare it with the period of a simple pendulum 0.50 m long, and explain the difference.

rubric.criterion: Finds T = 2π√(I/(Mgd)) = 1.31 s, compares it with 1.42 s for the simple pendulum, and explains that the rod's mass sits closer to the pivot, giving a smaller I relative to Mgd.

items.answer: (a) I = 0.075 kg·m^2 and d = 0.35 m. (b) T = 1.31 s. (c) The simple pendulum's period is 1.42 s, longer; the rod puts part of the mass nearer the pivot.
steps: Rod about its end: ML^2/3 = 0.025 kg·m^2; ball: mL^2 = 0.050 kg·m^2.
For a simple pendulum, I/(md) = L; here I/(Md) = 0.075/0.175 = 0.43 m, an equivalent length shorter than 0.50 m.
items.skill: Find the period of a composite pendulum

worksheets.title: Paper investigation: a torsion pendulum
worksheets.directions:
Paper investigation. This is a paper investigation with supplied, invented data. It does not replace the hands-on laboratory work, at least 25% of instructional time, that College Board's framework for the AP® Physics C: Mechanics course calls for, and it does not count toward the AP Course Audit or college lab credit. A horizontal bar hangs at its center from a thin vertical wire, as shown. When the bar is twisted through a small angle θ, the wire exerts a restoring torque τ = −κθ, where κ is the wire's torsion constant. Two small 0.200 kg masses are placed on the bar, one on each side, each at distance r from the wire. The student twists the bar about 20°, releases it, and times 10 oscillations for each r. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.
| r (m) | 0.050 | 0.100 | 0.150 | 0.200 | 0.250 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| time for 10 oscillations (s) | 19.8 | 25.2 | 32.1 | 39.6 | 48.0 |

items.prompt: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable, and two quantities the student must keep the same in every trial. Explain why the student timed 10 oscillations rather than one.
items.answer: Independent: the distance r of each mass from the wire. Dependent: the period T (from the time for 10 oscillations). Keep the same: the wire (its length and thickness, so κ), the two masses, the bar, and a similar starting twist. Timing 10 oscillations divides the reaction-time uncertainty of starting and stopping the timer by 10.
steps: The student chooses r and measures the time, so r is independent and T is dependent.
A timing uncertainty of about 0.2 s is 1% of a 19.8 s total but would be 10% of a single 2 s period.
items.skill: Identify variables and controls

items.prompt: Treating each mass as a particle, the rotational inertia is I = I_0 + 2mr^2, where I_0 is the bar's own rotational inertia. Starting from τ = −κθ, show that T^2 = (4π^2/κ)I_0 + (8π^2m/κ)r^2. What should the student graph to get a straight line, and what do its slope and intercept mean?
items.answer: From Iα = −κθ, ω^2 = κ/I and T = 2π√(I/κ), so T^2 = 4π^2(I_0 + 2mr^2)/κ. Graph T^2 against r^2: the slope is 8π^2m/κ and the intercept is 4π^2I_0/κ.
steps: Iα = −κθ has the form d^2θ/dt^2 = −(κ/I)θ, which is SHM with ω = √(κ/I).
Square T = 2π/ω and substitute I = I_0 + 2mr^2; T^2 is linear in r^2.
items.skill: Linearize a model

items.prompt: Compute T and T^2 for each trial and r^2 for each distance. Plot T^2 against r^2 on the grid provided, label and scale both axes, and draw a best-fit line.
steps: T is the time for 10 oscillations divided by 10; for example 32.1 s/10 = 3.21 s and (3.21 s)^2 = 10.3 s^2.
Choose scales so the points fill most of the grid, for example 0.0075 m^2 per column and 3 s^2 per row.
items.skill: Compute and plot linearized data

items.prompt: Use your best-fit line to find the torsion constant κ and the bar's rotational inertia I_0.

rubric.criterion: Finds a slope of about 317 s^2/m^2 (accept 300–335) from two points on the line, not two data points.
Uses slope = 8π^2m/κ to get κ = 0.050 N·m/rad (accept 0.047–0.053).
Uses intercept ≈ 3.1 s^2 = 4π^2I_0/κ to get I_0 ≈ 0.0040 kg·m^2 (accept 0.0035–0.0045).

steps: Least-squares slope 317 s^2/m^2 and intercept 3.13 s^2.
items.skill: Interpret slope and intercept

items.prompt: Each mass is really a small cylinder of radius 1.5 cm, not a particle. How does this change the graph and the values of κ and I_0 found from it?
items.answer: Each cylinder adds its own rotational inertia about its center, a constant that does not depend on r. That raises the intercept slightly but not the slope, so κ is unaffected and the fitted I_0 includes the cylinders' own inertia (about 2 × 10^−5 kg·m^2 each, under 1% of I_0).
steps: By the parallel-axis theorem each mass contributes I_cyl + mr^2, and I_cyl does not change with r.
For a uniform cylinder about its own axis, I_cyl = ½(0.200)(0.015)^2 = 2.3 × 10^−5 kg·m^2.
items.skill: Analyze a model approximation

items.prompt: The stopwatch timing has an uncertainty of about ±0.2 s for each set of 10 oscillations. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in T^2 for the first trial, and state which trial's T^2 is least certain in percentage terms.
items.answer: About ±2% in T^2 for the first trial (±1% in T, doubled by squaring). The first trial, with the shortest time, has the largest percentage uncertainty.
steps: 0.2 s/19.8 s ≈ 1.0% in T, and squaring doubles a percentage uncertainty: about 2.0% in T^2.
The same ±0.2 s is a smaller percentage of the longer times, so later trials are more certain.
items.skill: Estimate measurement uncertainty

items.prompt: Describe a procedure, with the same apparatus and some extra wires, to test whether a wire's torsion constant is inversely proportional to its length. Say what you would vary, what you would measure, what you would graph, and what result would support the idea.
items.answer: Use wires of the same material and thickness but several lengths L. Keep the masses at a fixed r (so I is fixed) and time 10 oscillations for each L. Since T^2 = 4π^2I/κ, κ ∝ 1/L implies T^2 ∝ L: a graph of T^2 against L should be a straight line through the origin.
steps: Hold I constant so that any change in T comes from κ.
If κ = c/L, then T^2 = (4π^2I/c)L, a line through the origin; a nonzero intercept or a curve would contradict the idea.
items.skill: Design an investigation

weeks.title: Practice exam, self-scoring, and error analysis
weeks.objective: Take the full-length practice exam under timed conditions, score it with its scoring guidelines, record raw points by section and unit, and classify and correct each error so that the next week's review is targeted.

connection.before: The review weeks: Week 31 (Units 1–4) and Week 32 (Units 5–7 and experimental design).
connection.after: Week 34 turns this week's raw-point tally and error log into targeted review before the exam.

days: Section I of the practice exam: 42 multiple-choice questions in 85 minutes, with any calculator and the formula reference.

Section II of the practice exam: 4 free-response questions in 95 minutes (mathematical routines, translation between representations, experimental design and analysis, qualitative/quantitative translation).
Score both sections with the answer key and scoring guidelines; fill in the raw-point tally by section and by unit.
Error analysis: classify every missed point, then rework each missed question from a blank page.
Practice scoring free response with rubrics and correcting worked solutions (worksheets B and C); write a one-week review plan.
explanation: The practice exam follows the May 2027 format of the AP® Physics C: Mechanics exam. Section I has 42 multiple-choice questions in 85 minutes, about 2 minutes each. Section II has 4 free-response questions in 95 minutes: one mathematical routines question (10 points, about 20–25 minutes), one translation between representations question (12 points, about 25–30 minutes), one experimental design and analysis question (10 points, about 25–30 minutes) and one qualitative/quantitative translation question (8 points, about 15–20 minutes). Any four-function, scientific or graphing calculator is allowed in both sections. The real exam is hybrid digital, with multiple choice in the Bluebook app and free response in a paper booklet; this practice exam is printed. Take it in two sittings, one per section, with a timer and no notes beyond the formula reference.

Score Section I with the key, one point per correct answer and nothing taken off for a wrong answer, so never leave a question blank. Score Section II with the scoring guidelines: each rubric row is a separate point for a specific piece of reasoning, so award a row when the response shows that reasoning, even if a later arithmetic slip spoils the final number. Many rows ask for consistency with an earlier answer; if a part uses a wrong earlier result correctly, it can still earn its own points. Record raw points in the tally by section and by unit. Raw points are a practice tally only: they are not an AP score, and this course does not convert them to the exam's 1–5 scale or estimate a result.

Error analysis turns the tally into a plan. For every missed point, decide which kind of error it was: a concept error (the wrong physics, such as conserving kinetic energy in an inelastic collision); a representation error (misreading a graph or diagram, or swapping sine and cosine); a calculus setup error (integrating over the wrong variable or dropping a constant of integration); an algebra or arithmetic slip; a units or sign error; or a reading error (answering a different question from the one asked). Then rework the question from a blank page without looking at the key. Errors of the same kind that recur across units point to a skill to practice; errors clustered in one unit point to content to review.

Common errors in self-scoring: awarding a point because the final number matches when the reasoning the row requires is missing; refusing a point because the final number is wrong when the row credits only the setup; and treating timing problems as content problems. If you ran out of time, note which questions you skipped and whether you could have solved them, and practice pacing separately (worksheet A).

examples.prompt: Score this response. Question: A 0.20 kg block is released from rest at the top of a frictionless quarter-circle track of radius 0.50 m and slides to the bottom, where the track is horizontal. Find the block's speed at the bottom and the normal force on it there. Rubric (3 points): 1 point for using energy conservation, mgR = ½mv^2; 1 point for v = 3.1 m/s; 1 point for applying N − mg = mv^2/R at the bottom to get N = 3mg = 5.9 N. Student response: "mgR = ½mv^2, so v = √(2gR) = √(9.8) = 3.1 m/s. At the bottom, N = mv^2/R − mg = (0.20)(9.8)/0.50 − 1.96 = 1.96 N."
examples.answer: 2 of 3 points. The response earns the energy row and the speed row but not the force row, because it writes N = mv^2/R − mg instead of N − mg = mv^2/R. Correct answer: v = 3.1 m/s and N = 5.9 N, upward.
steps: Row 1: the response writes mgR = ½mv^2 explicitly, so it earns the point.

Row 3: at the bottom the net force points up, toward the center: N − mg = mv^2/R, so N = mg + 2mg = 3mg = 3(0.20)(9.8) = 5.88 N. The response subtracted the weight instead of adding it, a sign error, so it does not earn the row.
Check: the track must push harder than the weight at the bottom, because the block is accelerating upward, so 1.96 N (equal to the weight) cannot be right.

examples.prompt: Analyze this error. Question: A 12 kg box rests on a level floor (μ_s = 0.50). A worker pushes horizontally on it with 20 N, and it does not move. What is the friction force on the box? Student solution: "f = μ_sN = (0.50)(12)(9.8) = 59 N."
examples.answer: Concept error: μ_sN is the largest possible static friction, not its actual value. The box is at rest, so friction balances the push: 20 N, opposite the push.
steps: Classify: the physics principle is wrong, so this is a concept error, not arithmetic.
Static friction adjusts to whatever value keeps the surfaces from slipping, up to f_max = μ_sN = 59 N.
Here ΣF_x = 0 with a 20 N push, so f = 20 N; 20 N < 59 N, so the box indeed stays at rest.
Check: if friction were 59 N against a 20 N push, the box would accelerate backward, which is impossible from rest.

worksheets.title: Pacing set: mixed multiple choice
worksheets.directions: Work all six questions in 12 minutes, about 2 minutes each, the pace of Section I. Mark any question you guess on, then check it afterward. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A stone is thrown horizontally at 8.0 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. At what angle below the horizontal is it moving just before it lands?
steps: The vertical velocity at impact is √(2gh) = √(2(9.8)(20)) = 19.8 m/s; the horizontal velocity stays 8.0 m/s.
tan φ = 19.8/8.0, so φ = 68° below the horizontal. (22° is the angle measured from the vertical.)
items.skill: Find a projectile's impact direction

items.prompt: A hockey puck slides 30 m across level ice before stopping. Its initial speed was 8.0 m/s. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the puck and the ice?
steps: Work–energy: μ_k mg d = ½mv^2, so μ_k = v^2/(2gd).
μ_k = 64/(2(9.8)(30)) = 0.11; the mass cancels.
items.skill: Use work–energy with friction

items.prompt: A horizontal spring launcher gives a ball speed v when compressed by a distance x. Ignoring friction, what speed does it give the same ball when compressed by 2x?
items.answer: (A) 2v
steps: ½kx^2 = ½mv^2, so v is proportional to x.
Doubling x doubles v; the stored energy is four times as large.
items.skill: Scale a spring launch

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s catches up with a 1.0 kg cart moving at 1.0 m/s in the same direction on a level track, and the carts stick together. What is their speed afterward?
steps: v = 2.3 m/s. (1.7 m/s treats the carts as moving toward each other.)
items.skill: Apply momentum conservation

items.prompt: A uniform solid cylinder starts from rest and rolls without slipping down a ramp, dropping a vertical height of 0.60 m. What is its speed at the bottom?
steps: Energy: Mgh = ½Mv^2 + ½(½MR^2)(v/R)^2 = ¾Mv^2.
v = √(4gh/3) = √(7.84) = 2.80 m/s. (3.43 m/s ignores rotation; 2.42 m/s is a hoop; 2.90 m/s is a solid sphere.)
items.skill: Use energy for rolling

items.prompt: A block on a spring oscillates with an amplitude of 0.10 m and a period of 0.50 s. What is the magnitude of its greatest acceleration?
steps: ω = 2π/T = 12.6 rad/s, and a_max = ω^2A.
a_max = (12.6)^2(0.10) = 15.8 m/s^2. (1.26 is ωA, the greatest speed in m/s.)
items.skill: Find SHM maximum acceleration

worksheets.title: Scoring free response with a rubric
worksheets.directions: Each task below shows a short free-response question, its scoring rubric and an invented student response. Award points row by row, say which rows the response earns and why, and write a corrected final answer. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: Question: A ball is thrown straight up at 12 m/s from a balcony 8.0 m above the ground. How long after it is thrown does it hit the ground? Rubric (3 points): 1 point for a position equation with consistent signs, such as y = 8.0 + 12t − 4.9t^2 (up positive, origin at the ground); 1 point for setting y = 0 (or Δy = −8.0 m) and solving the quadratic, keeping the positive root; 1 point for t = 3.0 s. Student response: "Up is positive. −8.0 = 12t + 4.9t^2, so 4.9t^2 + 12t + 8.0 = 0 has no positive root; I'll use 4.9t^2 + 12t − 8.0 = 0, so t = [−12 + √(144 + 157)]/9.8 = 0.55 s."
items.answer: 1 point (the solving row). The equation gives gravity the wrong sign, so row 1 is not earned, and the final time is wrong. Correct: −8.0 = 12t − 4.9t^2, so 4.9t^2 − 12t − 8.0 = 0 and t = 3.0 s (2.99 s).
steps: Row 1: with up positive, the acceleration is −9.8 m/s^2, so the term is −4.9t^2; the response's +4.9t^2 is inconsistent with its own sign choice.
Row 2: the response does set up a quadratic and keeps the positive root, so it earns this row.
items.skill: Score kinematics reasoning with a rubric

items.prompt: Question: A 5.0 kg sled is pulled across level snow by a rope at 30° above the horizontal. The rope's tension is 20 N and μ_k = 0.10. Find the sled's acceleration. Rubric (3 points): 1 point for N = mg − T sin 30° = 39 N; 1 point for ΣF_x = ma with T cos 30° − μ_kN; 1 point for a = 2.7 m/s^2. Student response: "N = mg = 49 N, so friction is 4.9 N. ma = T cos 30° − f = 17.3 − 4.9, so a = 2.5 m/s^2."
items.answer: 1 point (the ΣF_x row). The normal force ignores the rope's upward pull, so row 1 and the final answer are not earned. Correct: N = 39 N, f = 3.9 N and a = 2.7 m/s^2.
steps: Row 1: the rope pulls up with T sin 30° = 10 N, so the floor pushes up less: N = 49 − 10 = 39 N. Not earned.
Row 2: the response writes ma = T cos 30° − f, the correct form, so it earns the row.
items.skill: Score a dynamics response with a rubric

items.prompt: Question: A 2.0 kg block moving at 6.0 m/s slides 4.0 m across a rough strip (μ_k = 0.25) and then onto a frictionless section, where it compresses a spring (k = 200 N/m). Find the spring's greatest compression. Rubric (3 points): 1 point for the work done by friction, −19.6 J; 1 point for setting the remaining kinetic energy equal to ½kx^2; 1 point for x = 0.40 m. Student response: "Friction does −μ_k mg d = −19.6 J, so K = 36 − 19.6 = 16.4 J. ½kx^2 = 16.4, so x = 16.4/100 = 0.16 m."
items.answer: 2 points (rows 1 and 2). The response forgets the square root at the end. Correct: x^2 = 16.4/100 = 0.164 m^2, so x = 0.40 m (0.405 m).
steps: Row 2: ½kx^2 = 16.4 J is the right energy statement, earned.
Row 3: 100x^2 = 16.4 gives x = √(0.164) = 0.405 m, not 0.16 m. A units check also catches it: J divided by N/m is m^2, not m.
items.skill: Score an energy response with a rubric

items.prompt: Question: Cart A (1.0 kg) moving at 4.0 m/s hits cart B (3.0 kg) at rest on a level track, and they stick together. How much kinetic energy is lost? Rubric (3 points): 1 point for momentum conservation giving v = 1.0 m/s; 1 point for the initial kinetic energy, 8.0 J; 1 point for the final kinetic energy, 2.0 J, and the loss, 6.0 J. Student response: "(1.0)(4.0) = (4.0)v, so v = 1.0 m/s. K before = ½(1.0)(4.0)^2 = 8.0 J. K after = ½(3.0)(1.0)^2 = 1.5 J, so 6.5 J is lost."
items.answer: 2 points (rows 1 and 2). The final kinetic energy uses only cart B's mass. Correct: K after = ½(4.0)(1.0)^2 = 2.0 J, so 6.0 J is lost.
steps: Row 1: earned; the joined carts have mass 4.0 kg and v = 1.0 m/s.
Row 2: earned; 8.0 J.
Row 3: after the collision both carts move together, so the moving mass is 4.0 kg: ½(4.0)(1.0)^2 = 2.0 J, and the loss is 8.0 − 2.0 = 6.0 J.
items.skill: Score a momentum response with a rubric

items.prompt: Question: A thin hoop of mass 0.50 kg starts from rest and rolls without slipping down a ramp, dropping a height of 0.40 m. Find its speed at the bottom. Rubric (3 points): 1 point for energy conservation that includes rotational kinetic energy, Mgh = ½Mv^2 + ½Iω^2; 1 point for I = MR^2 and ω = v/R; 1 point for v = 2.0 m/s. Student response: "mgh = ½mv^2, so v = √(2gh) = √(2(9.8)(0.40)) = 2.8 m/s."
items.answer: 0 points. The response treats the hoop as sliding without rotation, so none of the rows is earned. Correct: Mgh = ½Mv^2 + ½(MR^2)(v/R)^2 = Mv^2, so v = √(gh) = 2.0 m/s (1.98 m/s).
steps: Row 1: no rotational kinetic energy appears, so not earned.
Row 2: no rotational inertia or rolling condition appears, so not earned.
Row 3: v = √((9.8)(0.40)) = 1.98 m/s; 2.8 m/s is the frictionless sliding result.
items.skill: Score a rolling response with a rubric

items.prompt:
Question: A student hangs masses m from a spring and times its oscillations. Use the data to determine the spring constant by graphing. Rubric (3 points): 1 point for plotting T^2 against m with labeled, scaled axes; 1 point for a slope taken from a best-fit line; 1 point for k = 4π^2/slope, about 9.9 N/m. Student response: "From the last trial, k = 4π^2m/T^2 = 4π^2(0.40)/(1.27)^2 = 9.8 N/m."
| m (kg) | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.40 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T (s) | 0.65 | 0.90 | 1.10 | 1.27 |
items.answer: 0 points. The response uses one data point instead of a graph and a best-fit line, so none of the rows is earned, even though the number is close. Correct: T^2 = 0.423, 0.810, 1.21 and 1.61 s^2; the best-fit slope is about 3.97 s^2/kg, so k = 4π^2/3.97 = 9.9 N/m.
steps: The question asks for k by graphing, and every row depends on the graph.
A best-fit line averages the scatter in all four trials and shows the small intercept (about 0.02 s^2) that a single point hides; the intercept hints at the spring's own mass.
items.skill: Score an experimental-analysis response

worksheets.title: Error analysis and corrections
worksheets.directions: Each worked solution below contains exactly one error. Find the step with the error, classify it (concept, representation, calculus setup, algebra or arithmetic, units or signs, or reading the question), explain it, and give the corrected answer. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units. Give directions and slopes in degrees; measure angular positions, angular speeds and phases in radians. State your positive direction or sense of rotation where it matters, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2, Earth's mass 5.97 × 10^24 kg and Earth's radius 6.37 × 10^6 m where needed.

items.prompt: Question: A wheel of radius 0.25 m spins at 600 revolutions per minute. Find the speed of a point on its rim. Student solution: "ω = 600/60 = 10 rad/s, so v = ωr = (10)(0.25) = 2.5 m/s."
items.answer: Units error in the first step: 600 rev/min is 10 rev/s, not 10 rad/s. ω = 10 × 2π = 62.8 rad/s, so v = (62.8)(0.25) = 15.7 m/s.
steps: v = ωr requires ω in rad/s; one revolution is 2π rad.
ω = (600 rev/min)(2π rad/rev)(1 min/60 s) = 62.8 rad/s; v = 15.7 m/s.
items.skill: Correct a rotational unit conversion

items.prompt: Question: A particle's velocity is v(t) = 3.0t^2 − 2.0t, in m/s with t in seconds, and x(0) = 1.0 m. Find x(2.0). Student solution: "x(t) = 6.0t − 2.0, so x(2.0) = 10 m."
items.answer: Calculus setup error: the student differentiated v (getting the acceleration) instead of integrating it. x(t) = 1.0 + t^3 − t^2, so x(2.0) = 1.0 + 8.0 − 4.0 = 5.0 m.
steps: Position is the antiderivative of velocity plus the initial position: x(t) = x(0) + ∫ from 0 to t of v dt.
∫ from 0 to 2.0 of (3.0t^2 − 2.0t) dt = 8.0 − 4.0 = 4.0 m, so x(2.0) = 5.0 m. A units check flags the error: 6.0t − 2.0 has units of m/s^2.
items.skill: Correct an integration error

items.prompt: Question: A rope pulls a crate 3.0 m across a level floor with a 40 N force directed 25° above the horizontal. How much work does the rope do? Student solution: "W = Fd sin 25° = (40)(3.0)(0.423) = 51 J."
items.answer: Representation error: the component of the force along the displacement is F cos 25°, not F sin 25°. W = (40)(3.0) cos 25° = 109 J.
steps: W = F·d = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement, here 25°.
(40)(3.0)(0.906) = 109 J. Check: a nearly horizontal pull should do nearly the full 120 J, not less than half of it.
items.skill: Correct a component error in work

items.prompt: Question: A uniform 1.2 kg rod 0.75 m long is pivoted at one end, held horizontal and released. Find its angular acceleration just after release. Student solution: "τ = mg(L/2) = 4.41 N·m and I = ML^2/12 = 0.0563 kg·m^2, so α = 78 rad/s^2."
items.answer: Concept error: the rod turns about its end, so I must be taken about the end, I = ML^2/3 = 0.225 kg·m^2. Then α = 4.41/0.225 = 19.6 rad/s^2.
steps: Στ = Iα holds about the axis of rotation; ML^2/12 is about the center.
items.skill: Correct a rotational-inertia error

items.prompt: Question: What is the period of a simple pendulum 1.0 m long on the Moon, where g = 1.62 m/s^2? Student solution: "T = 2π√(g/L) = 2π√(1.62) = 8.0 s."
items.answer: The formula is inverted (a units error a dimension check catches): T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(1.0/1.62) = 4.9 s.
steps: √(g/L) has units of 1/s, so 2π√(g/L) is an angular frequency, not a period.
T = 2π√(0.617 s^2) = 4.94 s; it is longer than on Earth (2.0 s) because gravity is weaker.
items.skill: Correct a formula with a units check

items.prompt: Question: A satellite orbits in a circle 400 km above Earth's surface. Find its orbital speed. Student solution: "v = √(GM/r) = √((6.67 × 10^−11)(5.97 × 10^24)/(4.0 × 10^5)) = 3.2 × 10^4 m/s."
items.answer: Reading error: r is the distance from Earth's center, R_E + 400 km = 6.77 × 10^6 m, not the altitude. v = √(GM/r) = 7.67 × 10^3 m/s.
steps: Gravity depends on the distance between centers, so r = 6.37 × 10^6 + 0.40 × 10^6 = 6.77 × 10^6 m.
v = √(3.98 × 10^14/6.77 × 10^6) = 7.67 × 10^3 m/s. Check: 32 km/s exceeds Earth's escape speed, so no satellite could orbit that fast.
items.skill: Correct a radius error in an orbit

weeks.title: Targeted review from practice-exam results
weeks.objective: Use the practice exam's raw-point tally and error log to choose review targets, and strengthen the three skills that most often cost points across units: choosing a principle and a system, setting up the calculus, and checking answers with units, limits and special cases.

connection.before: Week 33's practice exam, raw-point tally by section and unit, and error log.
connection.after: The exam falls about now; Weeks 35–36 follow it with synthesis investigations and a bridge to further physics.

days: Read the tally and error log: list the two units with the most missed points and the two most frequent error types; rework those questions.
Choosing a principle and a system in multi-stage problems (worksheet A).
Setting up integrals and derivatives: dm, dx, dt and dθ elements (worksheet B).
Checking answers: units, limiting cases, special cases and reasonableness (worksheet C).
A short mixed timed set in the weakest units, then a final pass through the formula reference.
explanation: Start from evidence. The practice-exam tally shows raw points by unit, and the error log shows what kind of mistake cost each point. Two patterns call for different work. If the missed points cluster in one unit, review that unit's ideas and rework its questions. If the same kind of error appears in several units (a sign convention, a missing rotational term, a calculus setup), practice that skill on fresh problems across units, because it will keep costing points wherever it appears. Spend most of the week on the two biggest targets rather than reviewing everything evenly.

Many problems run in stages, and each stage has its own principle. A block that slides down a frictionless ramp, collides with another block and then slides across a rough floor uses energy conservation, then momentum conservation (kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision), then the work–energy theorem with friction. Before calculating, label each stage with the principle and the system you are using, and name the quantity that carries from one stage to the next, usually a speed. In rotation, collisions with a pivot conserve angular momentum about the pivot, and a swing before or after uses energy.

Calculus setup questions reward a clear element. To integrate, picture one small piece: a slice dm of an object at distance r from an axis (dI = r^2 dm), a short displacement dx over which a force does dW = F dx, a short time dt over which a force delivers dJ = F dt, or a small angle dθ over which a torque does dW = τ dθ. Write the piece's size in terms of one variable (for example dm = λ dx, or dm = ρπr^2 dz for a disk-shaped slice), choose limits that cover the whole object or interval, and only then integrate.

Checks catch errors that rereading misses. Units: every term in a sum must have the same units, and the answer must have the units the question asks for. Limiting cases: set a mass, an angle or a friction coefficient to zero or to a very large value and see whether the expression gives the obvious answer (an Atwood machine with equal masses must not accelerate; an incline at 90° with no normal force must give free fall). Reasonableness: compare sizes with familiar ones (a car does not stop from highway speed in 1 m; no satellite orbits faster than escape speed). Common errors in review weeks are spreading time thinly over every unit, rereading notes instead of solving fresh problems, and skipping the checks under time pressure.
